Agree a two-minute review with two questions only: what actually happened, and what would a kind observer say. Then a physical switch. Practice on the last event the client replayed.

fields.label: The event I keep replaying
What I replay most (a sentence, a look, a pause)
My two-minute review: what actually happened
What a kind observer would say
My switch when the two minutes are up
How long the replay used to last, and how long it lasted this time

title: Social Prediction Log
summary: Records the client's forecast before a social situation and the outcome after, to compare over weeks.
goal: Build the client's own evidence that their predictions run far worse than events.
body_md: The forecast must be specific and rated: they will notice me blushing and think less of me, seventy percent. Afterward the client records what observably happened, not how it felt. Review the gap across ten entries, which is usually where belief shifts rather than in any single event.

fields.label: The upcoming situation
What I predict will happen, specifically
How sure I am (0-100%)
What observably happened
How I know (what people said or did)
How the prediction compared
What I predict next time, adjusted

title: Conversation Toolkit Card
summary: A pocket card of openers, follow-up questions and graceful exits for social situations.
goal: Reduce the load of inventing conversation so the client can practice being in it.
body_md: Build it with the client's own words, not scripts from a book, and include exits, since knowing they can leave makes staying easier. Warn against using it as a safety behavior: the card is for learning, and the goal is to need it less. Rehearse a full opener-question-exit in session.

fields.label: Three openers I could actually say
Three follow-up questions that work in most conversations
Two ways to leave a conversation gracefully
What I will do with my hands
The one I will try first this week
How it went, and whether I needed the card

title: Social Brave Steps for Teens
summary: A teen's own ladder of social situations from easy to hard, with a brave step per week.
goal: Give a teenager a graded, self-chosen path back into the social situations they have been dodging.
body_md: Let the teen build and order the steps; a ladder chosen by an adult will not be climbed. Keep parents to a support role agreed on the sheet. Steps should be specific: ask one question in class, not participate more. Celebrate attempts, not outcomes, and expect a step to be repeated before moving up.

fields.label: Situations I have been avoiding
My ladder, easiest at the bottom
This week's step
What I am afraid will happen
What actually happened
What my parent will do (and not do) to help
The step for next week

title: Continuing Bonds Letter
summary: A letter to the person who died, about what has happened since and what the client still carries of them.
goal: Support an ongoing connection with the person rather than a closing of the door.
body_md: Offer it as one option among several, since some clients find writing to the dead unbearable and others find it the only thing that helps. Frame the bond as something that changes rather than ends. The client decides whether to read it aloud, keep it, or take it somewhere. Include 988 among the prompts for the darkest hours.

fields.label: What I want to tell you about since you died
What I have kept of you (a habit, a phrase, an object, a way of seeing)
What I wish I had said
What I think you would say to me now
How I will keep you in my life going forward
If the grief ever gets dangerously dark: 988 (call or text), and who else I will reach

title: Grief Triggers Calendar
summary: A year at a glance with the dates, seasons and events likely to bring the grief up hard.
goal: Let the client see the hard days coming and plan support for them instead of being ambushed.
body_md: Include the obvious dates and the sideways ones: the first snow, the tax season the person used to handle, the song at the store. Plan for the week before an anniversary, which is often worse than the day. Decide with the client who will know about each date.

fields.label: Anniversaries and birthdays
Seasons, holidays and rituals that will be different
Sideways reminders I can predict
The next hard date, and what I will do that day
Who will know it is coming
What helped on the last hard date, and what did not

title: Dual Process Week Planner
summary: A week planned with time for facing the loss and time for the ordinary business of living, both on purpose.
goal: Normalize moving between grief and daily life instead of feeling guilty about either.
body_md: Explain that healthy grief moves between the loss and the rest of life, and that neither side is avoidance. Clients stuck on one side feel guilty when they laugh, or numb when they cannot cry; the planner gives both permission. Keep the entries small and concrete.

fields.label: Times this week I will let myself be with the loss (looking at photos, visiting, talking about them)
Times this week I will do ordinary or even pleasant things
The side I tend to get stuck on
What guilt says when I switch sides
What I will say back to it
How the week went

title: Memory Box Project
summary: A child decorates a box and fills it with objects, drawings and stories that hold the person who died.
goal: Give a grieving child a concrete, permitted place for their memories and a way to talk about them.
body_md: Let the child lead on what goes in and what stays private. Each item comes with a story the child tells if they want to; the telling is the work. Involve the surviving parent or carer where possible, and coach them to follow the child's pace rather than their own. Revisit the box on hard dates.

fields.label: What my box looks like
The first three things I put in it, and why
A story that goes with one of them
Something I want to ask about the person who died
Who I can open the box with
When I might want to open it

title: Grief Conversation Cards
summary: A deck of gentle prompts about the person who died, drawn in turn by family members or a group.
goal: Let a family or group talk about the person in a structured, low-pressure way.
body_md: Write the prompts with the group first so nothing on a card ambushes anyone, mixing light ones with heavier ones. Any card can be passed. Play in a circle with a talking object. In families, children often answer more freely than adults, which gives the adults permission.

fields.label: Prompts we put on the cards
The card I drew, and what I said
Something I learned about the person from someone else
A card I passed on
The card I would like to answer next time

title: Needs Inventory for Partners
summary: Each partner lists their needs in the relationship, ranked, and guesses their partner's list before comparing.
goal: Replace assumed needs with stated ones, and show each partner what the other has been guessing.
body_md: Have both partners complete it separately, including the guess about each other, before any discussion. The gaps between the guess and the real list are the material. Keep the tone of curiosity when a partner's need surprises the other; surprise is information, not an accusation.

fields.label: My top five needs in this relationship, ranked
How well each is being met right now (0-10)
What I think my partner's top five are
What surprised me about their real list
One need of theirs I could meet better this month
One need of mine I will ask for directly

title: Perpetual Problems Sorter
summary: Sorts a couple's recurring arguments into the solvable and the perpetual, and plans a different approach to each.
goal: Stop a couple from trying to solve what needs managing, and from managing what could be solved.
body_md: List the arguments first, then sort. Perpetual problems come from differences in personality or values and will be there in ten years; the goal is dialogue and humor about them, not a fix. Solvable problems get a concrete plan. Most couples are relieved to hear that having perpetual problems is normal.

fields.label: Arguments we have more than once a month
Which of these come from a difference in who we are
Which could actually be solved with a plan
For one solvable problem: our plan
For one perpetual problem: what we can each accept
How we will talk about the perpetual one next time it comes up

title: Trust Rebuilding Steps
summary: A shared ladder of specific, observable actions that would rebuild trust after a breach, with a timeline.
goal: Turn a vague demand to earn trust back into steps both partners can see happening.
body_md: The hurt partner names what would help; the other partner says what they can commit to. Steps must be observable, since promises to change are not. Agree how long the checking phase lasts, because trust cannot rebuild under permanent surveillance. Review progress monthly in session.

fields.label: What was broken, in one sentence each
Actions that would help me trust again (specific and visible)
Which of these I can commit to, and when
What transparency looks like for now, and for how long
What I need to hear when I have a wobble
How we will mark progress

title: Communication Pattern Replay
summary: Replays one recent exchange line by line, with each partner naming what they meant and what they heard.
goal: Show a couple the gap between what was said, what was meant and what landed.
body_md: Pick a short exchange, not the biggest fight. Write the actual lines, then have each partner add what they meant and what they heard. The gaps are usually where the fight lives. Finish by rewriting two lines each, and rehearse the rewrite in session.

fields.label: The exchange, line by line, as it happened
For my lines: what I meant
For their lines: what I heard
Where the gap between meant and heard was widest
Two lines I would rewrite
How the rewritten version sounds out loud

title: Relationship Values Compass
summary: Each partner names the kind of partner they want to be, separately from how the other is behaving.
goal: Anchor each partner to their own values so change does not wait on the other person moving first.
body_md: Works with a couple or with one partner alone. The key move is separating my values as a partner from what I get back; clients often discover they have been acting on a scoreboard. Choose one valued action for the week that does not depend on the other person's response.

fields.label: The partner I want to be, in three words
How I have actually been acting lately
What I have been waiting for my partner to do first
One valued action I will take this week regardless
What my mind says will happen if I go first
What actually happened

title: Safety and Stabilization Plan
summary: A plan for the practical and emotional safety a survivor needs in place before any deeper work.
goal: Put steady ground under the client first: who, where, what, and what to do when it gets too much.
body_md: Complete it together in session and never as homework. Cover present-day safety from the person who harmed them, the people who help, the skills that bring them back, and what to do in the worst hours. Move at the client's pace and do not ask for the details of what happened; that is not what this sheet is for. Include 988.

fields.label: Am I safe from the person now? What would make me safer
People I trust, and what each one can help with
Skills that bring me back when I am flooded
Signs that I am doing too much too fast
What I will do in the worst hour: 988 (call or text), and my other numbers
What I want my therapist to know about pace
What I am not ready to talk about yet, and that is fine

title: Consent and Boundaries Map
summary: Maps the client's yes, no and maybe across touch, closeness and conversation, in their own words.
goal: Help a survivor reclaim the right to decide, in small everyday ways, what they allow and what they do not.
body_md: Keep it to everyday boundaries at first: hugs, sitting close, questions from family, who has their number. The maybe column matters, since survivors often feel boundaries must be absolute to count. Rehearse one no in session. Nothing here asks about the abuse itself.

fields.label: Things I am a clear yes to
Things I am a clear no to
Things that are a maybe, and what would make them a yes
A boundary someone in my life keeps crossing
How I will say no to that, in my words
What I will do if they push
Someone who respects my boundaries well

title: Shame Response Sheet
summary: Catches the self-blame that follows abuse, tests it against what the client would say to another survivor, and writes the fairer version.
goal: Loosen the belief that the client caused, allowed or deserved what happened.
body_md: Do this in session, gently, and expect the double standard to be stark: the client will extend to another survivor a compassion they refuse themselves. Do not argue the client out of the belief; let the comparison do the work, and rate belief before and after. Stop if the client becomes flooded and return to grounding.

fields.label: What I tell myself about why it happened
How much I believe that (0-100%)
What I would say to a friend who told me the same story
Where the blame actually belongs
The fairer statement, in my words
How much I believe the fairer statement now (0-100%)

title: Support Disclosure Planner
summary: Plans whether, who, when and how much to tell, so a disclosure happens on the client's terms.
goal: Keep the choice of who knows, and how much, in the survivor's hands.
body_md: Not telling is a valid outcome of this sheet and should be said out loud. Work through what the client wants from telling, who is likely to respond well, and how much to say; a first sentence and an exit line are worth rehearsing. Plan for the reaction being disappointing, since it sometimes is.

fields.label: What I hope telling someone would give me
People I might tell, and how I think each would respond
The person I would tell first, if anyone
How much I want to say (a sentence is enough)
My first sentence
How I will end the conversation if I need to
What I will do for myself afterward, whatever their reaction

title: Body Safety Rules Poster
summary: A child makes a poster of body safety rules: private parts, okay and not-okay touch, secrets versus surprises, and who to tell.
goal: Teach a child the words and the permission to tell, as part of prevention work with families.
body_md: A prevention and education tool, done with a parent in the room where possible. Use correct names for body parts. Teach that surprises are fun and short and secrets about bodies are never kept. List five trusted adults. If a child discloses during this, stop the activity, stay calm, believe them, and follow your mandated reporting duties.

fields.label: Private parts have proper names, and mine are
Okay touch and not-okay touch: my examples
The difference between a surprise and a secret
My five trusted grown-ups
What I say if someone breaks a body safety rule
Where my poster will hang

title: Coping Menu by Situation
summary: A menu of the client's coping options sorted by where they are: at work, in public, at home, in bed.
goal: Match skills to settings so the right one is available where the distress actually happens.
body_md: Most clients have skills that only work at home and distress that happens elsewhere. Sort by setting and check that each setting has at least two options that are invisible to other people. Include one for the middle of the night. Keep the menu in the phone's notes.

fields.label: At work or school: two things I can do without anyone noticing
In public: two options
At home: two options
In bed at 3 a.m.: two options
The skill I reach for too often, and where it does not work
The new skill I will try this week, and where

title: Skill Practice Log
summary: A weekly log of which coping skill the client used, in what situation, and how well it worked.
goal: Turn coping from a vague resolve into a tracked practice with results.
body_md: The rating is the useful part: a skill that scores three out of ten in three different situations can be retired without guilt. Look for the mismatch between skills tried and situations faced. Praise the attempt, especially when the skill did not work, since trying is what builds the habit.

fields.label: Date and the situation
Distress before (0-10)
The skill I used
Distress after (0-10)
How well it worked (0-10) and why
A skill I could have used instead
The skill I will practice most next week

title: Coping Ladder for Kids
summary: A ladder of a child's coping moves from small feelings at the bottom to big ones at the top.
goal: Match the size of the coping move to the size of the feeling, in a picture a child can use.
body_md: Draw a ladder with three or four rungs and let the child assign feelings sizes to each. Small feelings get small moves: a breath, a drink of water. Big feelings get big moves: a break, a grown-up. Practice one move per rung in session and have the parent post the ladder at home.

fields.label: Bottom rung: a small feeling and my small move
Middle rung: a medium feeling and my medium move
Top rung: a huge feeling and my biggest move
How I know which rung I am on
Who helps me on the top rung
Where my ladder is posted

title: Coping Skills Relay
summary: Teams race to act out or demonstrate a coping skill for each situation card drawn.
goal: Rehearse coping skills under mild pressure and laughter, so they are practiced rather than just known.
body_md: Write situation cards with the group beforehand: a test tomorrow, a friend ignoring a text, a loud house. A team scores when the skill fits the situation and could actually be done there. Judge fit, not speed, and let the group argue the call; the argument is the learning.

fields.label: Situation cards we made
Skills my team demonstrated
A skill another team showed that I want to steal
A situation none of us could match well
The skill I will practice this week

title: Helpful vs Costly Coping Sort
summary: Sorts everything the client does to feel better into what helps in the long run and what costs more than it gives.
goal: Help the client judge coping by its long-term workability rather than by how fast it works.
body_md: List everything without judgment first, including the ones the client is ashamed of; those are usually the fastest-acting. Sort by long-term workability, not by how they look. Most clients find a few things belong in both columns depending on amount, which is worth writing down rather than resolving.

fields.label: Everything I do to feel better, fast or slow
Which ones help me next week too
Which ones cost more than they give
Which ones depend on how much
One costly one I will shrink, and how
One helpful one I will do more of, and when

title: Phobia Prediction Tracker
summary: Records what the client expects to happen around the feared object or situation and what actually occurs.
goal: Build the client's own evidence that the feared outcome and the felt danger diverge.
body_md: Ask for the specific feared outcome, not just fear: I will faint, the dog will bite, the plane will crash. Rate belief before and after each approach. The pattern across entries is what changes belief, so aim for at least eight entries before drawing conclusions together.

fields.label: The feared thing and the situation
What I predict will happen, specifically
How sure I am (0-100%)
Peak fear (0-10)
What actually happened
What I did during the peak
My belief in the prediction now (0-100%)

title: Approach Steps Planner
summary: Plans the next approach step toward a feared object in detail: where, how long, with whom, and what to drop.
goal: Make each approach step concrete enough to actually happen this week.
body_md: One step at a time, planned to the minute. Include what safety moves the client will drop, since carrying the escape plan into the step blunts it. Decide in advance how long to stay: long enough for the fear to fall, not just to touch and run. Debrief in session before planning the next.

fields.label: This week's step
Where and when, exactly
Who will be there, and what they will and will not do
How long I will stay (until fear drops by half)
The safety moves I will not use
What happened, and what I will do next week

title: Phobia Body Response Sheet
summary: Names what the client's body does around the feared thing, and separates the alarm from the danger.
goal: Help the client see the fear response as an alarm that can fire without a fire.
body_md: Map the response: heart, breath, muscles, stomach, the urge to run. Explain plainly that the body's alarm is doing its job and that the job is to get them out, which is why staying feels wrong. For blood or needle fears, note the faint response and plan applied tension separately.

fields.label: What my body does first around the feared thing
What it does next
The urge that comes with it
What the alarm is trying to make me do
What I know about the real danger in this situation
What I will do with the alarm next time it fires

title: Brave Practice Chart for Kids
summary: A sticker chart for a child's repeated brave practices with a feared thing, tied to a small reward.
goal: Make repetition of approach steps visible and rewarding for a child.
duration: 20 minutes to set up, then daily
body_md: Choose practices small enough to repeat daily: look at a picture of a dog, stand in the doorway with the lights off. Stickers go on for attempts, not for calm. Parents hold the chart and the reward and keep their own anxiety out of the practice. Change the practice when it stops earning fear.

fields.label: My brave practice this week
Stickers I earned
How scared I was the first time (0-10) and the last time
My reward when the chart is full
What my grown-up does during practice
Next week's brave practice

title: Fear Ladder Card Sort
summary: Situations written on cards and physically sorted into a ladder from least to most scary.
goal: Build a fear hierarchy as a hands-on sorting task rather than a form.
body_md: Write one situation per card with the client, at least fifteen, then sort them on the table or floor. The physical sorting draws out distinctions a form misses, and the client can move cards as beliefs change. Photograph the finished ladder and use it to choose the next approach step.

fields.label: Situations we wrote on cards
The bottom three cards
The top three cards
Cards I moved while sorting, and why
The card I will start with
The card I cannot imagine reaching yet

title: Body Neutrality Practice
summary: Daily short statements about what the body did today rather than how it looked.
goal: Move the client's relationship with their body from judgment toward function and use.
duration: Two minutes daily for two weeks
body_md: Aim for neutral, not positive; clients who cannot believe their body is beautiful can believe it carried them up the stairs. Keep the statements about doing and feeling. Notice when the client sneaks an appearance comment in and gently redirect. Never mention weight, shape or food in this practice.

fields.label: Three things my body did for me today
One thing it let me feel (warmth, music, a hug, the wind)
A neutral statement about my body, without judgment either way
What my mind wanted to add about how it looks
How I responded to that
The statement I will use tomorrow morning

title: Body Checking Log
summary: Records the mirror checks, pinching, comparing and photo scrutiny that keep body worry alive, and what each one did to mood.
goal: Show the client how checking feeds the worry, and plan a reduction.
body_md: Checking feels like getting information but produces worse mood almost every time; the log makes that visible. Include the quiet forms: reflections in windows, comparing in group photos, clothes tried and discarded. Plan one check to cut in half, not to stop entirely.

fields.label: Date and time
What I checked, and how (mirror, pinch, photo, comparing)
What I was looking for
Mood before and after (0-10)
How long the reassurance lasted, if any
The check I will cut in half next week
What I will do instead in that moment

title: Appearance Assumptions Sheet
summary: Lists the client's rules linking appearance to worth, acceptance or success, and tests each one.
goal: Loosen the beliefs that make appearance carry the whole weight of self-worth.
body_md: Draw out the if-then rules: if I looked different, then people would... Test each against the client's own experience and the people they admire. The goal is to shrink the share of self-worth that appearance holds, which a pie chart of what makes up their worth can show before and after.

fields.label: My rules about appearance (if I looked..., then...)
Where each rule came from
Evidence from my own life for and against it
People I admire, and how much their looks have to do with it
How much of my self-worth appearance holds now (%)
What else I would like it to rest on

title: Body Gratitude Function List
summary: A list of what the client's body has carried them through, by life stage, written as a record rather than a rating.
goal: Build a history of the body as a companion rather than an object under review.
body_md: Move through life stages: childhood play, illness survived, work done, people carried, places reached. The tone is a record, not a pep talk. Clients with a history of harming or overworking their body may find this tender; slow down there. No comments on shape or size anywhere on the sheet.

fields.label: What my body did for me as a child
What it has carried me through
What it lets me do that I would miss
Someone it has held or helped
Something it recovered from
What I would like to thank it for, plainly

title: Media Diet Audit
summary: An inventory of the accounts, shows and images the client consumes, and what each does to how they feel in their body.
goal: Change what the client feeds their body image, since much of it arrives through a screen.
body_md: Go through the phone together. For each account or habit, ask what it does to the client's body feeling in the ten minutes after. Unfollowing is a real intervention and often the fastest one; replace, do not just remove, so the feed is not empty. Repeat in a month.

fields.label: Accounts and shows I see most
How I feel in my body after each (better, worse, nothing)
The ones that leave me comparing
Accounts I will unfollow or mute this week
What I will follow instead (bodies doing things, other interests entirely)
How my feed feels after the change

title: Session Agenda Setter
summary: A short worksheet for bringing one or two items the client wants to cover before a session starts.
goal: Use it to give the client a stake in the hour and keep session time from drifting to whatever comes up last.
body_md: Hand this to the client a few minutes before the session, or have them fill it out in the waiting room; the two-item cap keeps someone who tends to arrive with a long list from using the whole hour on the first topic. Some clients leave it blank out of habit, so a verbal prompt at check-in works as well as the paper does. Keep it visible during the hour as a light anchor to return to if the conversation wanders.

fields.label: What is the one thing you most want to talk about today?
What is a second thing, if there's time?
Is there anything urgent that can't wait until later in the session?
How much time do you think each item needs?

title: Readiness and Confidence Ruler
summary: A 0-to-10 scale worksheet rating how important a change feels and how confident the client is that they can make it.
goal: Use it to open a conversation about ambivalence and turn a stuck should into a concrete next step.
body_md: Ask the client to mark where they land right now on two separate 0-to-10 lines, one for importance and one for confidence, then ask why they picked that number and not one lower; the answer surfaces their own reasons for change instead of the clinician's. A low confidence score next to a high importance score points straight at what to problem-solve next. Revisiting the same two lines across sessions shows movement a client might otherwise miss.

fields.label: On a scale of 0 to 10, how important is this change to you right now?
What made you pick that number instead of a lower one?
On a scale of 0 to 10, how confident are you that you could make this change?
What would move your confidence up by even one point?
What might get in the way?

title: Habit Stacking Planner
summary: A worksheet for anchoring a new habit to a routine the client already does every day.
goal: Use it to help a change stick by attaching it to an existing cue instead of relying on memory alone.
body_md: Have the client list three routines they already do without fail, such as making coffee or sitting down at their desk, and pick one to attach the new habit to immediately after. The habit should take under two minutes at first; ambition here works against the client, since a stack that takes too long gets skipped on a busy day. Check back the following week on whether the anchor held or whether a different routine would work better.

fields.label: What are three things you already do every day without having to think about it?
Which one of those could you attach a new habit to?
What is the smallest version of the new habit you could do right after it?
What might make you skip the anchor routine itself on a hard day?
How will you notice and restart if you miss a day?

title: Guilt and Shame Sorter
summary: A sorting worksheet that separates guilt about a specific action from shame about the self as a whole.
goal: Use it to help a client tell the two apart so guilt can lead to repair instead of curdling into shame.
body_md: Walk the client through a recent situation twice: once naming the guilt sentence, I did something wrong, and once naming the shame sentence, I am something wrong, then ask which one is actually true given what happened. Most people arrive fused, so slowing down to write both versions side by side is often the first time a client sees that only the first one points anywhere useful. A client who insists the shame sentence is simply a fact is worth a full session of its own before rushing to the repair step.

fields.label: What happened, in a few plain sentences?
What is the guilt sentence: what did you do?
What is the shame sentence: what does it say about you as a person?
Looking at both sentences, which one is actually supported by what happened?
If it's the guilt sentence, what's one step toward repair?

title: Self-Compassion Break Card
summary: A pocket card walking the client through a three-step self-compassion break in the middle of a hard moment.
goal: Use it to give the client something brief enough to reach for in the moment, not just after the fact.
body_md: Teach the three steps in session first: naming that this is a hard moment, remembering that struggle is part of being human, and offering a hand or words the kind of comfort a friend would get, then send the card home as a reminder rather than a script to read cold. Some clients resist the second step, insisting their situation is uniquely bad; naming that resistance is useful material, not a sign the exercise failed. A short practice run in session helps the card trigger a memory of doing it, not a new task.

fields.label: Name what's happening: what would you say to yourself right now?
Remind yourself: how is this moment connected to being human, not just you?
Offer yourself something kind, in the words or gesture you'd give a friend.
What changed, even slightly, after the three steps?

title: Double Standard Technique
summary: A dialogue worksheet comparing what the client tells themselves to what they'd tell a friend in the same spot.
goal: Use it to expose a harsh self-judgment by testing it against the standard the client already applies to others.
body_md: Ask the client to write their self-critical thought word for word, then write what they'd say to a close friend who told them the exact same thing about themselves. The gap between the two columns is usually the whole point; most clients spot it without being told, which lands harder than the clinician naming it for them. If the client insists their own case is genuinely different from a friend's, ask what specifically makes it different rather than accepting the claim at face value.

fields.label: What is the exact thought you have about yourself right now?
If a close friend told you they were thinking that about themselves, what would you say back to them?
What's different about your two answers?
What would it take to believe your own answer about the friend?

title: Problem-Solving Steps Guide
summary: A step-by-step worksheet for defining a problem, generating options, and picking one to try.
goal: Use it to slow down a client who jumps straight to worry or avoidance instead of working the problem itself.
body_md: Work through the steps in order: state the problem in one specific sentence, list every option without judging it yet, weigh the realistic ones, pick one, then set a date to check how it went. Clients often want to skip straight to solutions or generate only good options, so hold them to a genuinely wide brainstorm before any evaluating starts. This fits problems that are actually solvable; a worry with no real decision point underneath it is better routed to a worry or acceptance tool instead.

fields.label: State the problem in one specific sentence.
List every option you can think of, even bad ones; don't filter yet.
Which two or three options are realistic given your situation?
Which one will you try first, and when?
How will you know, and when will you check back, on whether it worked?

title: Point-Counterpoint Technique
summary: A two-column dialogue exercise where the client argues both for and against a rigid core belief out loud.
goal: Use it to loosen a core belief that's held up to logic but hasn't budged in daily life.
body_md: The clinician or the client takes the point side, voicing the belief as strongly as it actually feels, while the other takes counterpoint, arguing back with the client's own lived evidence; switch roles partway through so the client also has to argue against the belief in their own voice. This works best after questioning has already surfaced some counter-evidence, since the exercise is about practicing conviction, not discovering it fresh. Stop if it turns into the client simply restating the belief louder; that's a cue to slow back down to gathering evidence.

fields.label: State the belief exactly as it feels true, as strongly as you can.
Now argue back against it using something you actually know from your own life.
Switch roles: argue for the belief, then argue against it in your own voice.
Which side felt more convincing, and why?

title: Self-Instructional Training Script
summary: A script the client writes and rehearses to talk themselves through a stressful task step by step.
goal: Use it to replace spiraling self-talk with a planned, neutral narration the client can lean on under pressure.
body_md: Have the client write out the stressful task in stages, preparing, starting, handling a setback partway through, and finishing, with one calm, instructional line for each stage, the way a coach would narrate rather than the way an anxious inner voice usually does. Rehearse it out loud in session at least once before it goes home, since reading it silently doesn't build the same automatic reach for it under pressure. Revise the setback line often; it's usually the one that gets skipped and the one the client needs most.

fields.label: What is the stressful task, in one sentence?
What will you say to yourself while preparing for it?
What will you say to yourself right as you start?
What will you say to yourself if something goes wrong partway through?
What will you say to yourself once it's done?

title: Habit Reversal Training Log
summary: A tracking log pairing early awareness of an unwanted habit with a planned competing action.
goal: Use it to build the moment-to-moment awareness a client needs before a competing response can interrupt a habit.
body_md: Start with awareness alone for the first few days: the client simply logs each time they notice the habit starting, without yet trying to stop it, so they learn to catch it earlier each time. Once catches happen reliably before the habit is underway, add the second column and have the client swap in one specific competing action, such as clenching a fist or pressing their tongue to the roof of their mouth, every time they catch the urge. Progress is usually uneven; a bad day is data about a trigger, not a sign the log isn't working.

fields.label: What time did you notice the habit starting, or about to start?
What was happening right before you noticed it?
Did you catch it before, during, or after it started?
If you used the competing action, what did you do instead?
What made this catch easier or harder than usual?

title: Chinese Finger Trap Metaphor
summary: A hands-on demonstration of how straining against an unwanted feeling only pulls it tighter.
goal: Use it to help a client feel why easing into a feeling loosens it faster than fighting it does.
body_md: Bring an actual finger trap if you have one, or have the client mime pulling apart clasped hands; pulling outward against the resistance tightens the grip, just as straining against an unwanted feeling or urge tends to pull it tighter. Guide them to press gently inward instead and notice the slack that opens, then name a feeling or urge in their week where the same pulling shows up. Keep it brief and physical rather than letting it turn into explanation, and close by naming one small step toward something they value, even with the feeling still there.

fields.label: What did you notice in your body as you pulled against the trap?
Where in your week do you catch yourself pulling against a feeling or urge the same way?
What happens if you ease in instead of pulling away?
What is one step you could take toward something that matters to you, even with the feeling still there?

title: Joe the Bum Metaphor
summary: A short story about an unwelcome houseguest that reframes fighting a feeling as making room for it instead.
goal: Use it to shift a client from evicting a feeling to letting it stay while life goes on around it.
body_md: Tell the client about a host at a party when a loud, unwelcome guest shows up at the door; the host can spend the night trying to force the guest out, missing the party in the process, or let the guest stay in the corner while everyone else keeps mingling. Ask the client to name the feeling, urge or memory that is their own uninvited guest, and where they usually spend energy trying to throw it out. Clarify that letting the guest stay is not agreeing with it, just making room so the party can continue, then connect it to what hosting their own life would look like this week.

fields.label: Who or what is the unwelcome guest showing up at your door lately?
What does trying to throw the guest out usually look like for you?
What would it look like to let the guest stay in the corner while you keep hosting?
What is one part of your own party you'd like to get back to this week?

title: Radio Doom and Gloom
summary: A defusion exercise that has a client name their harshest inner commentary like a radio station playing on.
goal: Use it to help a client notice a running stream of self-criticism as a broadcast, not a fact.
body_md: Ask the client to picture their harshest inner commentary as a radio station playing in the background, and have them give it a name such as Radio Doom and Gloom, plus a tagline it might use to introduce itself. Practice noticing when the station switches on during the day and naming it, silently or out loud, rather than arguing with what it says or getting hooked. Watch for clients who turn the exercise into fighting the station; the aim is not to shut it off but to notice it is playing while still choosing what they do next.

fields.label: What would you name your mind's harshest radio station?
What is a tagline that station uses to introduce itself?
When did you notice the station switch on this week?
What did you choose to do while it was playing?

title: Eulogy Values Exercise
summary: A guided reflection where a client imagines what they would want said about them to surface what matters.
goal: Use it to help a client separate their real values from the goals or approval driving today's choices.
body_md: Have the client close their eyes or write in silence while you read a short prompt: imagine a gathering years from now where people who matter most are speaking about the life they lived, and picture what they hope is said about how they showed up, treated people and spent their time. Let them draft a few lines in that voice, then compare it to how they are actually spending this week. The exercise can surface grief or regret quickly, so slow the pace for a client carrying loss and keep the focus on direction, not scorekeeping.

fields.label: What do you hope is said about how you treated the people around you?
What do you hope is said about how you spent your time and energy?
Where does this week's schedule already match that? Where does it not?
What is one small shift that would bring this week closer to that direction?

title: Pink Elephant Suppression Exercise
summary: A one-minute thought-suppression demonstration that shows a client how trying not to think something backfires.
goal: Use it to make the cost of thought control concrete before shifting the work toward willingness.
body_md: Ask the client to close their eyes for one minute and try as hard as they can not to think about a pink elephant, then check in on how often the elephant showed up anyway. Draw the parallel to the effort the client puts into pushing away an unwanted thought, feeling or memory in daily life, and ask where trying not to think about it tends to backfire the same way. Some clients treat this as a party trick rather than personal data, so slow down and connect it directly to a thought or urge they actually struggle with, then use it as the bridge into practicing willingness instead of control.

fields.label: How many times did the pink elephant show up during the minute?
What thought, feeling or memory do you usually try hardest not to think about?
What has trying not to think about it cost you?
What would it look like to let the thought be there without fighting it?

title: IMPROVE the Moment Skills Card
summary: A card walking a client through each letter of IMPROVE for getting through an intense moment.
goal: Use it to give a client a menu of ways to ease a hard moment when the crisis has not fully passed.
body_md: Walk the client through each letter of IMPROVE, imagery, meaning, connection to something larger, relaxation, one thing at a time, a brief vacation, and encouragement, and have them write one concrete example next to each letter rather than leaving it generic. Practice one or two of the strongest fits out loud in session so the client has already rehearsed the motion before they need it. Watch for clients who fill in all seven from habit without noticing which ones actually shift their body; a shorter, practiced list beats a full card nobody can recall under pressure.

fields.label: Imagery: what picture could you call up that helps you feel steadier?
Meaning: what meaning or silver lining, if any, could you find in this moment?
Connection: what larger sense of support could you lean on right now?
Relaxation: what in your body could you loosen or soften right now?
One thing at a time: what is the single next thing in front of you?
Vacation: what would a five-minute break from this look like?
Encouragement: what would you say to a friend in this exact moment?

title: Turning the Mind Practice
summary: A repeated-choice practice where a client turns their mind back toward accepting a hard fact each time it drifts.
goal: Use it to build the muscle of choosing acceptance again and again rather than expecting it to stick once.
body_md: Have the client picture a fork in the road where one path is fighting a fact and the other is accepting it as it is right now, without that meaning they approve of it. Ask them to physically turn their body or hands toward the accepting path each time they notice themselves back on the fighting one, repeating the turn as many times as it takes rather than treating one turn as final. Normalize that most people turn their mind dozens of times over one hard fact, and that this is practice, not failure; pair it with a specific situation from the client's week.

fields.label: What is the fact or situation you keep fighting against?
What does the fighting path usually sound like in your head?
What does turning toward acceptance look or feel like for you?
How many times did you notice yourself turning back this week?

title: THINK Skill Practice Card
summary: A card that walks a client through THINK to build empathy for someone who irritated them before they respond.
goal: Use it to slow a client down between a trigger and a response by working through each letter of THINK.
body_md: Have the client pick a recent moment someone irritated or angered them, then walk through THINK: think about what the other person might have been feeling, build empathy for their situation, notice interpretations being jumped to, look for kindness that could be offered instead, and consider how the client would want to be seen if roles were reversed. Encourage more than one interpretation of the other person's behavior, since the exercise loses power if the client settles on the first, least generous read. Works best once a conflict has cooled enough to reflect, not relitigate.

fields.label: What did the other person do that irritated or angered you?
What might they have been thinking or feeling in that moment?
What is one kinder interpretation of their behavior, even if you're not sure it's true?
What would kindness look like in your response?
How would you want to be seen if you were in their position?

title: Build Mastery Activity Log
summary: A weekly log for scheduling one activity that stretches a client's skill just past what feels comfortable.
goal: Use it to build a client's sense of competence as a buffer against emotional vulnerability over time.
body_md: Have the client pick one activity a day that is slightly harder than what already feels easy but still realistic to finish, not something so far out of reach that it sets them up to quit. Log the activity, how it went, and a one-line note on what it showed them they can do, building toward a felt sense of competence rather than perfection. Coach clients away from picking only chores or only enjoyable activities; the skill is specifically about a stretch, so a walk that runs a little longer or a hard conversation practiced out loud both count as long as it pushes just past the current edge.

fields.label: What activity did you pick for today, and why does it stretch you slightly?
How did it actually go?
What did finishing it show you that you can do?
What will tomorrow's slightly harder step be?

title: Mindfulness of Current Emotion Log
summary: A log for observing and naming a strong emotion as it moves through the body without pushing it away.
goal: Use it to build a client's capacity to stay with a feeling long enough to watch it change on its own.
body_md: When a strong feeling shows up, have the client pause, name it as specifically as they can, and locate where it shows up in the body, then simply observe it rising, peaking and settling the way a wave does, without pushing it away, holding onto it or acting on the urge that comes with it. Remind them the feeling is not who they are; it is something moving through them right now. Clients often try to reason their way out of the feeling instead of observing it, so redirect gently back to sensation and breath.

fields.label: What emotion showed up, named as specifically as you can?
Where did you feel it in your body?
What did you notice as you watched it rise and then start to settle?
What urge came with it, and did you act on it or just notice it?

title: Digital Boundaries Agreement
summary: Partner A and Partner B each name one phone habit that gets in the way of connection.
goal: Use it to turn recurring phone friction into one specific agreement both partners chose together.
body_md: Have each partner pick just one habit rather than a full list, or the conversation turns into a grievance session. The agreement should be specific and revisited in a month — vague promises like less phone time rarely hold, while phones stay in the kitchen after nine does. Watch for one partner using the exercise to score points about the other's habits instead of naming their own.

fields.label: One screen habit of mine that gets in the way
One screen habit of my partner's that gets in the way
What I need instead, in one sentence
What my partner needs instead, in one sentence
Our specific agreement, with a time and place
How we will check in on this in one month

title: In-Law Boundary Script
summary: The couple writes a script together for a specific extended-family boundary, spoken and supported.
goal: Use it to turn a vague complaint about in-laws into a boundary both partners can say out loud.
body_md: Name the actual situation, not the general in-law relationship — a holiday visit, a phone call, an unsolicited comment. The partner whose family it is usually needs to deliver the boundary, with the other partner's support named out loud beforehand so it does not surface as a fight later. Rehearse the exact line in session before it gets said at home.

fields.label: The specific situation this boundary covers
The boundary, in one sentence
Who will say it, in their own words
How the other partner will show support beforehand
What we will do if it is not respected

title: Financial Values Interview
summary: Each partner interviews the other with structured questions about their money history and worries.
goal: Use it to surface the beliefs about money that drive conflict before the couple sets a shared plan.
body_md: Run this before any budgeting conversation — couples who jump straight to numbers often skip the history that explains why a figure feels threatening to one partner and neutral to the other. Ask partners to interview each other rather than fill it out separately, and to listen for the feeling behind each answer more than the number. Save actual budget talk for a later session.

fields.label: What money meant in your family growing up
A money memory that still affects you
What feels safe about how we handle money now
What feels risky about how we handle money now
One thing you want your partner to understand about your money worries
One shared money value we already agree on

title: Date Night Menu Builder
summary: Each partner lists low-cost, low-effort ways to connect, then the couple builds a shared menu.
goal: Use it to make time together the default instead of something the couple negotiates every week.
body_md: Couples who have stopped dating often cannot picture what to do together anymore, so start with a long list before narrowing it down. Ask each partner to include at least one option under fifteen minutes for weeks with no time to spare. Post the finished menu somewhere visible at home so choosing becomes picking from a list rather than a new conversation every time.

fields.label: My ideas for a full evening together
My ideas for fifteen minutes or less
My partner's ideas for a full evening together
My partner's ideas for fifteen minutes or less
Our shared menu, in order of how often we want to use it

title: Sleep Territory Negotiation
summary: The couple maps their mismatched sleep habits and negotiates specific changes to try.
goal: Use it to turn nightly sleep friction into agreed experiments instead of a recurring resentment.
body_md: Mismatched bedtimes, temperature, noise and snoring are common and rarely named directly because they feel too small to raise — until they are not. Have each partner describe their ideal sleep setup without editing it for the other, then negotiate one or two concrete changes to try for a week, from separate blankets to a later shared bedtime. Frame it as logistics, not a verdict on the relationship.

fields.label: My ideal sleep setup, if I am honest
My partner's ideal sleep setup, as I understand it
What currently disrupts my sleep
What currently disrupts my partner's sleep
One change we will try this week
How we will check whether it helped

title: Turn-Taking Traffic Light Craft
summary: The child colors a paper traffic light to signal when they can wait, slow down or go.
goal: Use it to give a young child a visual cue for waiting and impulse control during play.
body_md: Have the child color and cut out the three traffic light circles, then keep the finished light where play happens. The parent's job is to hold it up silently during turn-taking moments — board games, siblings, waiting for a snack — rather than narrating instructions, so the child starts reading the cue instead of a lecture. Young children often need the yellow step named out loud the first few times before it sticks.

fields.label: What red (stop and wait) looks like for me
What yellow (slow down) looks like for me
What green (my turn) looks like for me
One place at home we will use the light
Parent: how will you hold up the light without talking?

title: Friendship Recipe Card
summary: The child decorates a recipe card listing the ingredients of a good friend.
goal: Use it to give a child concrete, memorable language for friendship skills.
body_md: Let the child pick the ingredients first — sharing, listening, saying sorry, taking turns — before helping them write measurements like a cup of listening or a pinch of patience, and decorate the card like a real recipe. The parent's role is to reference the finished card by name during an actual friendship moment that week, rather than filing it away, so the language becomes something the family actually uses.

fields.label: Ingredients for a good friend
The recipe, in my own words
A time I used one of these ingredients
A time a friend used one on me
Parent: one moment this week to point back to the recipe

title: Mistake Monster Craft
summary: The child draws and decorates a silly monster that stands for their fear of getting things wrong.
goal: Use it to externalize a young child's fear of mistakes into something they can talk back to.
body_md: Have the child give the monster a name, a color and a ridiculous detail or two — the sillier it looks, the easier it is to talk back to later. Once it exists on paper, practice a line the child can say to it out loud, like mistakes help me learn. The parent's job is to name their own small mistakes out loud during the week and show how they handle them, since children copy the response more than the words.

fields.label: My mistake monster's name and what it looks like
What my mistake monster says to me
What I say back to it
A mistake I made this week and what happened next
Parent: a mistake you will name out loud this week

title: Kindness Chain Craft
summary: The child builds a growing paper chain, adding one link for every act of kindness they notice.
goal: Use it to make a young child's kind actions visible and countable over a week.
duration: Fifteen minutes to start, then daily
body_md: Cut a stack of colored paper strips ahead of time so adding a link takes seconds. A link can be an act of kindness the child did or one they received — both count, since noticing kindness from others matters as much as doing it. The parent's role is to ask one specific question at the same point each day, like at dinner, so the habit of noticing has a fixed home rather than depending on the child remembering alone.

fields.label: Today's kind act — what I did
Today's kind act — what someone did for me
How adding the link felt
How many links are on our chain now
Parent: the daily moment we will check in

title: Listening Ears Headband Craft
summary: The child builds a paper headband with big ears, then plays a short listening game wearing it.
goal: Use it to make active listening a physical, playful skill a young child can practice and name.
body_md: Have the child decorate the ears before the game starts, then take turns: one person tells a short story while the ear-wearer repeats back one detail before responding. Keep each turn under a minute so the exercise stays a game rather than a drill. The parent's job is to model getting a detail wrong and fixing it, so the child sees that listening well is a skill you build, not something you either have or do not.

fields.label: What I remember from the story I heard
One detail I almost missed
How it felt when someone listened to me
Parent: one moment you got it wrong and fixed it
One time this week we will wear the ears again

title: Silent Line-Up Challenge
summary: The group lines up in order by a trait, like comfort with uncertainty, without speaking.
goal: Use it to surface how a group reads each other nonverbally and where assumptions creep in.
body_md: Call out a trait to line up by — most to least comfortable with change works well — and set the rule that no one may speak, write or mouth words; gestures only. Give the group two minutes, then have them call out their guessed order before revealing the real one by a quick show of hands. Debrief on where the guessed order was wrong and what cue people used instead of asking directly, since that gap is usually the most useful part.

fields.label: The trait we lined up by
Where I placed myself
Where the group guessed I was
What surprised me about the actual order
What we relied on instead of asking

title: Values Tug of War
summary: Two players hold a rope, each naming a value they are pulling toward, then debrief the pull.
goal: Use it to make the physical feeling of competing values concrete before talking them through.
body_md: Give each player one end of a soft rope and one value to hold, such as honesty versus keeping the peace, then let them pull at a comfortable effort for thirty seconds while the group watches. Stop before anyone strains and switch pairs and values each round. The debrief question that matters most is what it felt like to give an inch versus hold firm, and whether that matches how the person handles the real version of that pull.

fields.label: The two values in our round
Which side I pulled
What holding firm felt like
What giving an inch felt like
A real situation this pull reminds me of

title: Two-Minute Partner Interview
summary: Pairs interview each other for two minutes on a prompt, then introduce their partner to the group.
goal: Use it to build a group's habit of listening for detail instead of preparing what to say next.
body_md: Pair people up, give both partners the same prompt card, and time two minutes each way with a visible timer so no one has to guess when to switch. The rule for the introduction round is that each person may only share what their partner told them, not add their own commentary, which keeps the exercise about listening rather than performing. Debrief on what was hard to remember and what it felt like to be introduced by someone else's words.

fields.label: The prompt we used
What my partner told me
What I noticed I almost forgot
How it felt to be introduced in someone else's words
One thing I want to remember about my partner

title: Devil's Advocate Debate Cards
summary: Small teams argue an assigned side of an everyday dilemma, then swap and argue the other side.
goal: Use it to loosen a group's grip on being right by making flexible thinking part of the rules.
body_md: Draw an everyday dilemma card — texting an ex, calling out a friend, splitting a bill unevenly — and assign each team a side regardless of what they actually believe. Give three minutes to build the strongest case, then swap sides and argue the opposite. The debrief question to press on is which side was harder to argue and what that says about where a person's thinking gets stuck, more than which side won.

fields.label: The dilemma we debated
The side I was assigned first
My strongest point for that side
What changed when I argued the other side
Which side was harder to argue, and why

title: Mirror Match Warm-Up
summary: Partners silently mirror each other's slow movements, then switch who is leading.
goal: Use it to build a group's attunement to nonverbal cues before a harder conversation.
body_md: Pair people facing each other and set one clear rule: the leader moves slowly enough that the follower can match in real time, no fast or surprising movements. Switch leaders halfway through without announcing it and see how quickly the pair notices the switch. Debrief on how it felt to lead versus follow and whether the pair matched each other's pace evenly, since that unevenness often shows up again in how the group talks.

fields.label: Who led first in my pair
How it felt to lead
How it felt to follow
When we noticed the switch
How evenly we matched each other's pace

title: Felt Safety Inventory
summary: A worksheet that lists the people, places, and sensations that help a client feel safe today.
goal: Use it to build a ready list of present-day safety resources for moments when arousal spikes.
body_md: Keep every item anchored in the present, a person, place, or sensation available right now, rather than anything tied to the event itself; if a memory surfaces, gently redirect back to what feels safe in this room. Some clients freeze on the first line, so offer easy prompts like a pet, a blanket, or a doorway in view. Let the list grow slowly across sessions instead of rushing to fill every row in one sitting.

fields.label: List three people you feel safe with right now.
List three places where your body feels calmer.
Name a sound, texture, or object that helps you feel grounded.
What is one small thing you could do today to feel a little safer?
Who could you call or text if things start to feel too big?

title: Dual Awareness Practice Sheet
summary: A CBT worksheet that pairs a present-moment anchor with a felt sense of distress so both can be held at once.
goal: Use it to build the client's capacity to notice activation while staying oriented to the here and now.
body_md: Walk the client through naming one current stressor or body sensation alongside a present-moment anchor, the chair under them, the room's temperature, a sound nearby, so neither the distress nor the present gets pushed away. This is a stabilization skill, not a review of what happened, so redirect firmly if the client starts narrating the event; keep the focus on right now. Some clients need the anchor named first and the sensation second until the pairing feels steadier.

fields.label: What sensation or feeling do you notice in your body right now?
What is one thing you can see in the room right now?
What is one thing you can feel with your hands right now (chair, fabric, table)?
On a scale of 1 to 10, how activated does your body feel right now?
What helped you feel even slightly more here, in this room?

title: Safe Enough Activity Ladder
summary: An ACT ladder that paces a return to valued activities at whatever speed still feels safe enough.
goal: Use it to help the client reconnect with valued activities without pushing faster than their system can tolerate.
body_md: Have the client list valued activities they have pulled back from since the event, then rank each by how safe enough it currently feels rather than by difficulty alone. The client commits to only the step that still feels manageable this week, and the clinician notes should flag that a stalled rung is information, not failure, so slow the pace rather than pushing through. Nothing here asks for narrative detail about what happened; the focus stays on values and pacing.

fields.label: What is one activity you used to enjoy that you have pulled back from?
On a scale of 1 to 10, how safe enough does trying a small piece of it feel this week?
What is the smallest version of that activity you could try?
What value does this activity connect to for you?
What support would make this step feel more doable?

title: Flashback Response Skills Card
summary: A pocket card of steps to use the moment a flashback or intrusive memory starts.
goal: Use it to give the client a rehearsed sequence for orienting back to the present during an intrusion.
body_md: Rehearse the sequence in session before the client carries the card: name today's date and location out loud, name five things they can see, press feet into the floor, and reach for a listed support contact if the intrusion does not ease. This is a stabilization card, not a place to record what the flashback was about, so keep every field oriented to the present moment and to actions. Practice it while calm first so the steps are familiar before they are needed under stress.

fields.label: What are three things you can see right now?
What is today's date and where are you right now?
What is one thing you can press your feet or hands against?
Who is one person you could contact if you need support?
What is one phrase that helps you feel more in the present, such as 'that was then, this is now'?

title: Partner Grounding Support Guide
summary: A couples worksheet that maps how a partner can help ground the other during a trauma response.
goal: Use it to give both partners a shared, rehearsed plan for support in the moment.
body_md: Have the partner who experiences activation name their early signals and what actually helps, while the supporting partner names what they can realistically offer and what to avoid, such as touch without asking first. Meet with both partners together so the plan is agreed rather than assumed, and steer away from any discussion of the event itself; this sheet is about the here-and-now response, not the history behind it. Revisit the plan every few months since signals and needs can shift.

fields.label: Partner one: what are your early signs that you are becoming activated?
Partner one: what specifically helps you feel safer in that moment?
Partner two: what can you offer when you notice those signs?
Partner two: what should you check with your partner before doing, such as touch?
Together: what is one signal or word you can use to ask for this support?

title: Worry Rocks Backpack
summary: A craft where a child sorts worry rocks into a backpack to carry and a jar to set down.
goal: Use it to help a child physically sort which worries are theirs to carry and which they can set aside.
body_md: Have the child decorate a small paper backpack and a jar, then write or draw one worry on each small paper rock. Together sort each rock into the backpack, worries the child can act on today, or the jar, worries that belong to a grown-up or can wait; the parent's role is to help name which rocks go where without dismissing any worry as silly. Some children want to keep every rock in the backpack at first, so revisit the sort over a few sessions rather than forcing it in one sitting.

fields.label: Draw or write one worry on a rock.
Is this worry something you can do something about today?
Who is a grown-up who could help carry this worry?
How does your backpack feel now, lighter or the same?

title: Odds Are Dice Game
summary: A dice game that compares a feared outcome's guessed odds with its realistic odds.
goal: Use it to build practice estimating real-world probability instead of worst-case certainty.
body_md: Each player names one feared outcome, rolls two dice, and states the number as their gut-feeling percent chance of it happening, then the group discusses a more realistic estimate together and the player rerolls to represent that number instead. Take turns through several rounds, and debrief on how it felt to sit with an estimate lower than the gut reaction. Keep the tone playful; if a player's fear feels too heavy for the game format, set it aside for individual work instead.

fields.label: Name one thing you are worried might happen.
What is your gut-feeling percent chance it happens?
What is a more realistic percent chance, based on past experience?
What would you do differently if you believed the realistic number?

title: What-If Spiral Map
summary: A worksheet that traces how one what-if thought spirals into the next so a client can find where to step off.
goal: Use it to help the client see the spiral's shape and choose one point to interrupt it.
body_md: Ask the client to write their starting what-if thought in the center, then branch out each thought that follows it, arrow by arrow, until the spiral runs its course. Once mapped, review the chain together and mark the earliest point where a different response was possible; that point becomes the target for a coping skill going forward. Some clients find the spiral speeds up as they write, which is useful information about how fast the pattern usually moves.

fields.label: Write your starting what-if thought.
What thought came right after that one?
Keep following the chain, what came next, and next?
Where in the chain could you have stepped off?
What is one thing you could do at that point instead?

title: Probability Overestimation Log
summary: A CBT log that compares a client's predicted odds of a feared outcome against what actually happened.
goal: Use it to give the client repeated evidence for recalibrating an overestimated probability.
body_md: Each time a feared prediction comes up, the client logs the predicted percent chance before the event and the actual outcome afterward, building a running record across the week. Review the pattern together in session rather than letting the client draw conclusions alone, since early entries can feel discouraging if the predicted number was high. Watch for clients who quietly skip logging the outcome when the prediction did not come true; that avoidance is itself worth naming.

fields.label: What are you predicting will happen?
What percent chance do you give it before it happens?
What actually happened?
How does the predicted number compare to what happened?

title: Worry Radio Station Practice
summary: An ACT defusion exercise that reframes anxious thoughts as a radio station playing worst-case broadcasts.
goal: Use it to build distance from anxious thoughts so the client can keep acting on their values while the station plays.
body_md: Have the client name their anxious inner voice as a radio station, Worry FM or similar, and practice noticing when it switches on without needing to turn it off first. Ask what it is broadcasting today, then ask what the client would do next if the station stayed on in the background rather than in the foreground. This is a noticing practice, not a debate with the content, so redirect gently if the client starts arguing with the broadcast instead of observing it.

fields.label: What would you name your worry station?
What is it broadcasting right now?
Can you let it play in the background while you do something else?
What is one thing you'd do next even if the station's volume stayed the same?

title: Build Mastery Step Plan
summary: A DBT worksheet that plans one small mastery activity a day to counter low mood.
goal: Use it to help the client schedule brief, achievable mastery activities and track the mood shift after each.
body_md: Draw on the DBT build-mastery skill: help the client pick one small, genuinely achievable task each day, something slightly challenging but not overwhelming, and log mood before and after completing it. Keep the tasks small on purpose; an overambitious goal that fails can reinforce low mood instead of easing it. Watch for clients who plan every task for the end of the week and prompt them to spread attempts across days instead.

fields.label: What is one small, doable task for today?
Rate your mood before starting, 1 to 10.
Rate your mood after finishing, 1 to 10.
What got in the way, if anything?
What task will you try tomorrow?

title: Low Mood Support Check-In
summary: A couples check-in that helps a partner share what low mood feels like today and what support would help.
goal: Use it to give both partners a structured way to name needs without one partner guessing or fixing.
body_md: The partner experiencing low mood names their energy level and one concrete thing that would help today, while the supporting partner reflects back what they heard before offering it; this stops well-meant fixing from landing as pressure. Run it as a short, regular check-in rather than only during a hard stretch, so it does not become a crisis-only conversation. Some couples fall into problem-solving too quickly; redirect back to listening first if that happens.

fields.label: Partner one: how is your energy today, on a scale of 1 to 10?
Partner one: what is one thing that would help today?
Partner two: what did you hear your partner ask for?
Partner two: what can you offer, realistically, today?
Together: when will you check in again?

title: Energy Battery Recharge Chart
summary: A chart where a child colors in their energy battery each day and picks a recharge activity.
goal: Use it to help a child notice low-energy days and connect them to one small, chosen activity.
body_md: Have the child color in a battery icon to show how full or empty they feel that day, then choose one activity from a menu they helped build, a short walk, a favorite song, a game with a parent, to recharge. The parent's role is to schedule that one activity into the day rather than leaving it to chance, and to color a battery of their own alongside the child so it feels shared rather than singled out. Keep the menu short and revisit it together every couple of weeks.

fields.label: Color in how full your battery feels today.
Pick one thing from your recharge menu to try.
Who will help you do it today?
How full does your battery feel after?

title: Tiny Wins Toss
summary: A toss game where each catch prompts a player to share one tiny win from their week.
goal: Use it to build practice noticing small effort and accomplishment that low mood tends to discount.
body_md: Players toss a soft ball around the circle; whoever catches it names one tiny win from the past week, no matter how small, getting out of bed on time counts as much as finishing a project. Keep turns quick and resist the urge to rank wins by size, since the point is building the habit of noticing rather than grading the outcome. Debrief by asking what it was like to hear everyone else's small wins, and whether any of their own surprised them once said aloud.

fields.label: What is one tiny win from your week?
What made that win possible?
What did it feel like to say it out loud?

title: Withdrawal and Return Map
summary: A worksheet that maps activities a client has withdrawn from and one small step back toward each.
goal: Use it to turn a long list of dropped activities into a short list of manageable next steps.
body_md: Have the client list activities they have quietly stopped doing since low mood set in, then, for each one, write the smallest possible version of returning to it rather than the full activity itself. Sort the list by how doable each small step feels right now, and pick only one or two to try before the next session. Clients often list steps that are still too large, so use the session to shrink them further rather than letting an ambitious plan set up another discouraging week.

fields.label: What is one activity you've pulled back from?
What is the smallest version of returning to it?
How doable does that small step feel, 1 to 10?
What might get in the way?
What would help you follow through?

title: If-Then Plan Builder
summary: A short worksheet that turns a vague intention into a specific if-then cue the client can act on right away.
goal: Use it to help a client turn a stalled intention into an automatic trigger for starting a task.
body_md: This tool is built on implementation intentions: instead of a vague goal like start my report, the client names a specific cue and a specific action, such as when I sit down after coffee I open the document and write one line. Have them write three of these in session and pick the one most likely to happen today. What trips people up is choosing a cue that is not reliably present, like when I feel motivated; push for a fixed time, place, or existing habit instead. Watch for plans stacked onto tasks the client tends to skip entirely.

fields.label: Write one task you keep putting off.
Name a cue that happens every day no matter what (a time, place, or habit).
Write your plan as: When [cue], I will [tiny action].
Write two backup cues in case the first one doesn't work.
What usually gets in the way of starting?

title: Values Over Urgency Sort
summary: A sorting exercise that separates tasks pulling for attention from the ones that actually matter to the client.
goal: Use it to help a client notice when urgency is driving their day instead of their own values.
body_md: The client lists everything competing for attention on a typical day, then sorts each item into loud and urgent or quiet and valued, noticing how often the loud pile wins even when the quiet pile matters more. In session, ask what it costs when a valued task keeps losing to a louder one. What trips people up is confusing urgency with importance; a notification and a values-linked task can both feel pressing in the body, so slow the client down to check which one actually connects to something they care about. Some clients need a shorter list to avoid overwhelm.

fields.label: List everything pulling for your attention on a typical day.
Circle the ones that feel loud and urgent, even if they don't matter much.
Underline the ones that feel quiet but connect to something you value.
Pick one quiet, valued task to protect tomorrow.
What usually happens when you try to protect it?

title: One-Mindfully Task Card
summary: A pocket card that walks a client through doing one task at a time when attention keeps splitting.
goal: Use it to help a client practice the one-mindfully skill on a single task instead of several at once.
body_md: The card gives the client three prompts for a task: name the one thing you are doing, notice when attention has moved elsewhere, and gently bring it back without self-criticism. Practice it in session on something boring, like folding a napkin, so the client feels the pull to multitask and the return in real time. What trips people up is expecting attention to stay put; the skill is the returning, not the staying, so normalize needing to return many times in one task. Keep the card visible, like on a desk or a phone lock screen.

fields.label: Name the one task you are about to do.
Set a short timer and start the task.
When your mind wanders, write down where it went.
Bring your attention back to the task without judging yourself.
How many times did you notice your attention move?

title: Task Handoff Agreement
summary: A short agreement that spells out how one partner hands a task to the other without it getting lost.
goal: Use it to help both partners agree on a clear handoff instead of relying on memory alone.
body_md: One partner often carries tasks in their head and forgets them mid-stream, while the other ends up frustrated by dropped follow-through; this agreement has both partners name one task being handed over, write what done looks like, and agree on a specific place it gets written down so neither is relying on memory. Run it in session so each partner hears how a missed handoff lands before it becomes a blame conversation at home.
