What trips people up is a vague handoff like can you deal with the mail; push for a concrete finish line and a day. Revisit the agreement after a week.

fields.label: Partner A: name one task you are handing over.
Partner A: what does finished look like?
Partner B: where will you write this down so you don't forget?
Both: by when will it be done?
Both: how will you check in without it feeling like a reminder?

title: Body Battery Check-In Chart
summary: A drawn battery icon a child colors in to show how much focus and energy they have left.
goal: Use it to help a child notice and name a dropping attention battery before it hits empty.
body_md: The child draws a battery icon and colors it in to match how full their focus feels right now, then the parent helps them name what usually drains it, like a loud room or a long worksheet, and what recharges it, like a movement break or a snack. Use simple, playful language and let the child pick their own colors and stickers. What trips people up is waiting until the battery reads empty to check in; coach the parent to ask for a check partway through homework, before frustration builds. Post the chart where the child can point to it instead of explaining in words.

fields.label: Draw your battery and color in how full it feels right now.
What usually makes your battery go down fast?
What helps your battery fill back up?
Draw a picture of your favorite recharge break.
Show a grown-up your battery today and tell them the number.

title: Urge Countdown Game
summary: A quick card game where players race to name a coping move before an urge's clock runs out.
goal: Use it to give a client fast practice matching an urge to a ready response before it fades or peaks.
body_md: Deal each player a card naming a common urge trigger, like boredom, a stressful call, or a specific place, and set a short timer for how long an urge typically holds before it eases; the player names a coping move out loud before time runs out, and the group can add options if stuck. Play several rounds, then debrief on which coping moves came to mind fastest and which triggers left the group blank. What trips people up is treating this as a quiz with one right answer; any response works as long as it does not involve substance use. Keep the tone light, not like a test.

fields.label: Write one urge trigger that shows up often for you.
Write the coping move you reached for fastest during the game.
Write a trigger that left you stuck, with no ready response.
Name one new coping move you heard from someone else that you'd try.
Where will you keep this list so it's handy when an urge shows up?

title: High-Risk Moment Map
summary: A worksheet that maps the times, places, and people linked to a rise in urges around substance use.
goal: Use it to help a client see the pattern behind their highest-risk moments instead of feeling ambushed by them.
body_md: The client fills in a grid crossing time of day, place, and who they were with for the last several moments an urge toward substance use spiked, then looks for repeats: a certain hour, an empty apartment, a specific friend. In session, ask what was happening emotionally in the hour before each moment, not just the moment itself, since urges build before they peak. What trips people up is listing only dramatic triggers and skipping quieter ones, like a slow afternoon with nothing planned; prompt for one low-key moment too. Use the map to plan around the riskiest windows, not willpower alone.

fields.label: List the last few times an urge to use spiked.
For each one, write the time of day and where you were.
For each one, write who you were with, if anyone.
What was happening in the hour before each spike?
Which time, place, or person shows up more than once?
What's one change you could make around your riskiest window?

title: Urge Intensity Timeline
summary: A tracking sheet that graphs how an urge's intensity rises and falls across its course.
goal: Use it to help a client see that an urge has a shape and an end, not a flat, unbroken pull.
body_md: Across a week, the client rates the intensity of urges tied to substance use on a zero-to-ten scale at set check-in points, whether or not they act on the urge, and plots the numbers to see the rise and fall rather than assuming it only climbs. Review the timeline together, pointing out the peak, how long it lasted, and the number twenty minutes later. What trips people up is checking in only during the worst moments, which makes urges look constant; ask for at least one calm-stretch rating too. Use the pattern to set realistic expectations for how long a client needs to ride out a spike.

fields.label: Rate your urge from zero to ten right now.
Write what's happening around you at this moment.
Rate the same urge again in twenty minutes.
What did you do while you waited it out?
Looking at today's numbers, when was the peak?

title: Room for the Urge Practice
summary: A short practice that has a client make space for an urge in their body instead of pushing it away.
goal: Use it to help a client hold an urge without fighting it or immediately acting on it.
body_md: Guide the client to notice where an urge tied to substance use shows up in the body, then, instead of tensing against it, have them breathe into that spot and imagine making room around it, the way you'd loosen a tight collar rather than pull it off. Say the urge's name softly, like there's an urge here right now, to build a gap between noticing it and acting on it. What trips people up is expecting the urge to vanish; the aim is coexisting with it a while, not eliminating it, so name that beforehand. Practice on a mild everyday urge first, like reaching for a phone, before a stronger one.

fields.label: Where in your body do you notice the urge?
Describe its size, shape, or temperature.
Say silently: there's an urge here, and I don't have to act on it.
Breathe into that spot for five slow breaths.
What did you notice change, if anything?

title: Urge Delay Card
summary: A pocket card that walks a client through delaying action on an urge in fifteen-minute steps.
goal: Use it to give a client a concrete way to put distance between an urge and a decision.
body_md: The card sets a fifteen-minute delay before the client acts on an urge tied to substance use, backed by a short list of distraction and soothing moves picked in session, like calling a support person, stepping outside, or running cold water over their hands. When the timer ends, the client rechecks the urge's intensity and either rides out fifteen more minutes or moves to a next step. What trips people up is picking distractions not actually available, like a hobby needing setup; keep the list short and reachable in under a minute. Practice picking an option before the client leaves.

fields.label: Write three things you can do in under a minute to distance yourself.
Write the name and number of one support person to call.
Set a fifteen-minute timer and try one option.
Rate the urge again once the timer ends.
What's your next step: another fifteen minutes, or calling your support person?

title: Anger Signals Check-In
summary: A short conversation guide where partners share their own early anger signals with each other.
goal: Use it to help both partners recognize the other's early warning signs before anger escalates.
body_md: Each partner separately names the physical and behavioral signs that show up before they get angry, like a tight jaw, going quiet, or talking faster, then the couple shares lists in session so both can start spotting the signal instead of only the blowup. Ask each partner what they'd want the other to do when they notice it, whether that's naming it gently or giving space. What trips people up is one partner using the list as ammunition later; frame it as information for care, not a scorecard. Have the couple keep both lists somewhere they can glance at during a tense moment.

fields.label: Partner A: what does your body do right before you get angry?
Partner A: what do you want your partner to do when they see that?
Partner B: what does your body do right before you get angry?
Partner B: what do you want your partner to do when they see that?
Both: what's one signal you never noticed in the other before today?

title: Mad Monster Mask Craft
summary: A child decorates a paper mask as their mad monster, then talks about what wakes it up and calms it down.
goal: Use it to give a child a playful, external character for talking about anger without feeling blamed.
body_md: The child draws and decorates a mask for their mad monster, choosing a face, colors, and a name, then the parent asks what wakes the monster up, what it wants to do when it's awake, and what helps it fall back asleep. Keeping the anger in the monster gives the child room to describe big feelings without feeling like they are the problem. What trips people up is a parent rushing to correct the child's description; let the story unfold first and save coaching for after the mask is finished. Keep the mask visible at home as a shared reference next time the monster shows up.

fields.label: Draw and decorate your mad monster's face.
Give your monster a name.
What wakes your monster up?
What does your monster want to do when it's awake?
What helps your monster calm down and go back to sleep?

title: Cool-Down Card Race
summary: A turn-based card game where players race through a set of cool-down steps before time runs out.
goal: Use it to give a client or group repeated, low-stakes practice moving through cool-down steps quickly.
body_md: Shuffle a deck of cards, each naming one cool-down step like naming the feeling, three slow breaths, or stepping away, and give each player a scenario card describing a moment that would spark anger; on their turn, a player draws cool-down cards and acts out each step against a short timer, racing to reach the last card before time runs out. Debrief on which steps felt easiest and which ones players wanted to skip. What trips people up is players rushing through steps without doing them; slow the pace and model one round yourself first. Keep scenario cards realistic to the group's own life.

fields.label: Write the anger scenario your card described.
List the cool-down steps in the order you used them.
Which step was hardest to actually do, not just say?
Which step do you think you'd reach for first in real life?
What would make that step easier to remember in the moment?

title: Anger Fuel and Fizzle Log
summary: A log that tracks what feeds an angry moment and what helps it fizzle out afterward.
goal: Use it to help a client separate what fuels their anger from what actually cools it down.
body_md: After an anger episode, the client logs what fueled it, like being interrupted or feeling dismissed, and separately logs what helped it fizzle, whether that was walking away, a text to a friend, or time passing. Over several entries, patterns surface: the same fuel showing up repeatedly, or a fizzle strategy that works more reliably than expected. What trips people up is logging only the fuel and skipping the fizzle, since that side often gets forgotten once the moment has passed; prompt for it the same day. Review the log every couple of weeks to sort out which fizzle strategies work.

fields.label: What happened right before you noticed anger building?
What fueled it, in your own words?
What did you do once you noticed it?
What actually helped it fizzle out?
Looking back, what fuel keeps showing up across entries?

title: Hostile Read Thought Check
summary: A quick check that tests a client's first hostile read of someone else's action against other explanations.
goal: Use it to help a client slow down an automatic hostile interpretation before it fuels anger.
body_md: When a client describes getting angry at someone's action, like being cut off in traffic or not getting a text back, have them write the automatic read first, usually something like they did that on purpose, then generate two other explanations that fit the same facts. Rate how believable each explanation feels and notice whether the anger shifts as the client works through the list. What trips people up is generating alternatives that still carry blame; push for one explanation that has nothing to do with the client at all. Practice on a recent lower-stakes moment before a harder one.

fields.label: What did the other person do?
What was your first read on why they did it?
Write two other explanations that fit the same facts.
Rate how believable each explanation feels, zero to ten.
Did your anger shift as you worked through the list?

title: The Certainty Trap Metaphor
summary: A metaphor exercise for the pull to grip harder at certainty about an intrusive thought.
goal: Use it to build willingness to sit with doubt instead of chasing certainty.
body_md: Introduce the trap metaphor before the exercise: the harder a client grips at certainty about an intrusive thought, the tighter the trap seems to close, the way wet sand squeezes through a clenched fist. Walk through moments the client notices themselves gripping, such as checking, asking or reviewing, and what loosening the grip could look like for even a few seconds. Some clients resist at first because letting go feels like giving in to the doubt; go slow and stay curious about that fear with them.

fields.label: Where does the urge to grip for certainty show up most in your week?
What does 'gripping tighter' look like for you — checking, asking, reviewing?
Describe a moment you loosened your grip on certainty, even briefly.
What did you notice in your body or mind when you loosened your grip?
What is one place this week you could practice loosening the grip on purpose?

title: Compulsion Opposite Action Plan
summary: A plan for practicing DBT's opposite action skill against a specific compulsive urge.
goal: Use it to help a client rehearse acting opposite to an urge to check, wash or repeat.
body_md: Have the client name one recurring urge — to check, wash, count or repeat — and describe the action the urge is pushing toward. Together define the opposite action: staying with the unlocked door, the imperfect email, the unwashed hands a little longer than feels tolerable. Rehearse the opposite action in session first when possible, then log real attempts through the week. Watch for the client quietly adding a mental compulsion, like silently repeating a phrase, in place of the physical one, and name that pattern if it shows up.

fields.label: Name the urge you are working with this week.
What is the urge pushing you to do?
What is the opposite action, in specific and doable terms?
How did the opposite action go when you tried it?
What got in the way, if anything, and what would help next time?

title: Partner Reassurance Response Plan
summary: A plan for how a partner responds to reassurance requests without feeding the cycle.
goal: Use it to help both partners agree on a kinder way to answer reassurance-seeking.
body_md: The requesting partner names the questions and reassurance-seeking they lean on most, and the other partner names how often they currently answer them and what that costs. Together they draft a short, warm script the answering partner can use instead of repeating the reassurance, along with a signal the requesting partner can give when the urge feels hardest to sit with. This works best introduced gradually rather than as an overnight switch, and the answering partner may need coaching on how to stay warm while still holding the new response.

fields.label: What questions or reassurance do you ask your partner most often?
Partner: how do you usually respond, and how does that leave you feeling afterward?
Draft the new short response your partner will use instead.
What signal will you give each other when the urge to ask or answer is strongest?
What would make it easier to stick with this plan on a hard day?

title: Doubt Detective Badge Craft
summary: A badge-making craft that casts a child as a detective who questions sneaky doubts.
goal: Use it to give a child a playful role for noticing and questioning intrusive doubts.
body_md: The child decorates a paper badge and names their detective persona, then draws or writes three clues, doubts that show up and try to trick them into checking or asking again. The parent helps the child practice a detective line, such as 'that doubt is not new evidence,' and wears the badge during a practice moment at home that week. Keep the tone playful rather than serious; the point is distance from the doubt, not winning an argument with it.

fields.label: Draw or write one doubt your detective badge is watching for.
What does this doubt try to get you to do?
What is your detective line for talking back to the doubt?
Parent: when did you see your detective use the badge this week?
What happened when the doubt got a detective line instead of a checking trip?

title: Doubt or Fact Card Sort
summary: A turn-based sorting game that separates sticky doubts from plain facts.
goal: Use it to build a light, shared vocabulary for spotting doubt versus fact in session.
body_md: Write a mix of statements on cards, some plain facts, some sticky doubts dressed up as facts, and shuffle the deck. Players take turns drawing a card, reading it aloud, and sorting it into a doubt or fact pile before the group votes; a correct guess earns a point, and a debate over a tricky card is where the real work happens. Close with a short debrief on which cards were hardest to sort and why doubts are built to feel convincing.

fields.label: Write one statement that felt like a fact but turned out to be a doubt.
What made that doubt so convincing in the moment?
Which card was hardest for the group to sort, and why?
What helps you tell a doubt from a fact outside of the game?

title: After the Panic Debrief Sheet
summary: A short debrief a client fills out once a panic episode has passed.
goal: Use it to review what preceded a panic episode and what helped it ease.
body_md: Fill this out with the client once the acute spike has passed, either in session or as soon after an episode as the client can manage. It separates what came before the episode from what the client tried during it and what actually seemed to help, so patterns become visible across several entries rather than staying a single blurry memory. Clients often underestimate how much already helped; point that out when the sheet shows it.

fields.label: What were you doing right before the episode started?
What did you notice first in your body?
What did you try while it was happening?
What seemed to help it ease, even a little?
What would you want to remember for next time?

title: Fear of Fear Prediction Log
summary: A log that tracks predictions about panic sensations against what actually happens.
goal: Use it to loosen the fear-of-fear cycle by testing predictions against outcomes.
duration: Five minutes per entry over two weeks
body_md: Panic often keeps itself going through a second layer of fear about the sensations themselves, the sense that a racing heart means something is badly wrong. Have the client write the exact prediction before a sensation escalates, rate how convinced they are, then log what actually happened once it passed. Reviewing several entries side by side, in session, tends to do more than any single one; watch for predictions getting vaguer over time as a sign the client is avoiding pinning them down.

fields.label: What sensation are you noticing right now?
What do you predict will happen if it keeps going?
How convinced are you of that prediction, from 0 to 100?
What actually happened once the sensation passed?
How does the outcome compare with the prediction?

title: Staying in the Storm Practice
summary: A willingness practice for staying present through a panic surge rather than fleeing it.
goal: Use it to build willingness to stay in a situation while panic sensations move through.
body_md: Introduce the storm as a metaphor for a panic surge: it builds, peaks and passes on its own timeline, and the client's job is not to stop the storm but to stay standing through it. Practice naming the urge to leave, run or fight the sensations the moment it shows up, and choosing one small willing action instead, like keeping both feet still. This is easiest to build gradually in low-stakes moments before asking a client to try it during a full episode.

fields.label: Describe a recent moment the panic 'storm' started building.
What was the urge telling you to do — leave, fight, distract?
What is one small willing action you could take instead of following the urge?
What did you notice about the storm's shape — building, peak, passing?
What would staying a little longer make possible for you?

title: Panic Reset Temperature Card
summary: A pocket card walking a client through a cold-temperature reset during a panic spike.
goal: Use it to give a client a fast physical reset to try when a panic spike feels overwhelming.
body_md: Cold water or an ice pack held to the face can shift the body's alarm response quickly during a sharp panic spike, and this card walks a client through the steps in order: where to hold the cold, how long, and what to expect as the surge starts to settle. Practice the steps in session so the sequence is familiar before a real spike, and check for any heart condition or other reason cold exposure would not be a fit before assigning it as homework.

fields.label: Where will you keep cold water or an ice pack accessible?
Walk through the steps you will take when a spike starts.
What did you notice in your body during and after using the card?
How long did it take for the spike to settle?
What would make this easier to reach for next time?

title: Partner Reassurance Cycle Map
summary: A map of how a partner's reassurance during panic keeps the cycle going for both of them.
goal: Use it to help a couple see and shift a reassurance pattern built up around panic episodes.
body_md: Draw the cycle together: the panicking partner's request for reassurance, the supporting partner's response, the short-term relief, and how the same request tends to return sooner and louder next time. Naming the pattern out loud often brings relief and some defensiveness at once, since the supporting partner has usually been doing what looked most caring. Close by drafting one small shift each partner is willing to try, such as a pause before answering or a shorter response.

fields.label: What does the request for reassurance usually sound like?
Supporting partner: what do you usually say or do in response?
How long does the relief tend to last before the request returns?
What is one small shift you are each willing to try?
What support would make that shift easier to hold to?

title: Family Feelings Check-In Wheel
summary: A spinning wheel craft the family points to for a quick feelings check-in together.
goal: Use it to build a quick, low-pressure habit of naming feelings as a family.
duration: 30 minutes to build, then a few minutes daily
body_md: The child decorates a paper wheel with feeling faces and a spinning arrow while the parent builds a matching one, and the family picks a daily moment, such as dinner, to each point to how they are feeling before talking about why. The parent's job is to model naming a hard feeling plainly, including their own, since children tend to match whatever level of honesty the adults show first. Keep entries short on busy nights rather than skipping the check-in altogether.

fields.label: Draw or write the feelings on your wheel.
Point to how you are feeling right now.
What is one reason you feel that way today?
Parent: what feeling did you point to, and what made that true today?
What was it like to hear how someone else in the family was feeling?

title: Special Time Roll and Play
summary: A roll-and-play dice game that turns one-on-one special time into a set of connection prompts.
goal: Use it to make regular one-on-one time easy to start and hard to skip.
body_md: Build a simple die or spinner labeled with six connection activities, a silly voice game, a drawing challenge, a pillow fort minute, and similar low-prep options, and let the child roll to pick what special time looks like that day. The parent's only rule during the roll is to follow the child's lead on the activity without correcting or directing it, even when the drawing is messy or the rules keep changing. End with a short debrief on what each of you liked best.

fields.label: What did you roll, and what did you choose to play?
Parent: what was hardest about following your child's lead today?
Child: what was your favorite part of special time today?
What would you want to roll again next time?

title: Positive to Corrective Ratio Tracker
summary: A daily tally of positive attention against corrective comments a parent gives a child.
goal: Use it to help a parent notice and shift the balance of positive to corrective attention.
duration: A few minutes daily for one week
body_md: Most parents estimate their ratio of praise to correction far more generously than a tally shows, so have the parent make simple hash marks through the day rather than trying to recall totals at night. A lopsided count is common and not a verdict on the parent; use it to find one or two moments a day where a specific, genuine positive comment could fit naturally. Revisit the tally weekly rather than daily so small shifts have room to show up.

fields.label: Tally each positive comment you gave today.
Tally each corrective comment you gave today.
What is one moment today a positive comment could have fit?
What got in the way of noticing positives in the moment?
What is one specific positive comment you will look for tomorrow?

title: Parent Guilt Thought Record
summary: A thought record for the guilt-driven thoughts that follow a hard parenting moment.
goal: Use it to help a parent examine guilt thoughts rather than simply carrying them.
body_md: Have the parent write the exact thought that followed a hard moment, snapping, missing a school event, losing patience, word for word rather than the general feeling of guilt. Walk through the evidence for and against the thought as written, and a more balanced version that still takes the moment seriously without inflating it into a verdict on the parent's whole character. Watch for the balanced thought sliding back into a harsher one by the next line; that slide is often the most useful part to discuss.

fields.label: What is the exact guilt thought, word for word?
What moment brought it on?
What evidence supports the thought?
What evidence works against the thought as written?
Write a more balanced version of the thought.

title: The Parent I Want to Be Compass
summary: A values exercise mapping the kind of parent a client wants to be against a hard week.
goal: Use it to reconnect a parent with chosen values after a week that felt off course.
body_md: Ask the parent to describe, in their own words, the kind of parent they want to be, warm, steady, playful, whatever fits, before looking at a specific recent moment that felt far from that. The gap is not evidence of failure; it is information about where a small committed action could point back toward the compass this week. Keep the chosen action small and concrete, since parents in this exercise tend to reach for something too large to sustain.

fields.label: In your own words, what kind of parent do you want to be?
Describe a recent moment that felt far from that.
What got in the way in that moment?
What is one small action this week that points back toward your compass?
What would help you remember this compass in a hard moment?

title: Radical Acceptance for the Birth You Had
summary: A DBT worksheet guiding a new parent through radically accepting a birth that didn't go as planned.
goal: Use it to help a client stop fighting a birth experience they can't change.
body_md: Walk the client through the steps of radical acceptance applied specifically to their birth experience: naming what happened, noticing where they are still arguing with reality, and practicing turning the mind toward acceptance without implying they have to approve of what happened. This tends to surface grief, anger, or guilt about interventions, a birth plan that changed, or feeling unheard by a care team, so pace it slowly and expect more than one pass. Watch for a client who equates acceptance with saying the birth was fine; the point is ending the internal fight, not endorsing it.

fields.label: What did you picture your birth being like, before it happened?
What actually happened, in your own words?
What part of it are you still arguing with or wishing you could redo?
What would it feel like to stop fighting that part, even for one minute?
What do you still need to grieve about how it went?

title: Postpartum Intimacy Reconnection Guide
summary: A conversation guide that helps new parents talk through changes to physical and emotional intimacy after birth.
goal: Use it to open a low-pressure conversation about intimacy before it becomes a silent sore spot.
body_md: Have each partner complete their half before talking, since postpartum bodies, exhaustion, and touch tolerance change fast and partners often assume the other feels the same way they do. One partner may be ready for touch sooner or later than the other, and both may be carrying unspoken worry about rejecting or pressuring the other. Name early on that intimacy includes non-sexual touch, and that the goal here is an honest baseline conversation, not a plan to fix anything by next week.

fields.label: What kind of touch feels good to you right now, and what feels like too much?
What has changed in how your body feels since birth that your partner should know?
What are you afraid your partner is thinking about this part of your relationship?
What is one small way you'd like more closeness this week, sexual or not?
What do you want your partner to know you need from them right now?

title: Becoming a Big Sibling Craft
summary: A craft activity where a child decorates a keepsake box for feelings about a new baby in the house.
goal: Use it to give an older sibling a hands-on way to name mixed feelings about a new baby.
body_md: The child decorates a small box, then the parent helps them add drawings or notes for feelings that come up about the new baby, including ones that feel less allowed, like jealousy or wanting less attention on the baby. Keep supplies open-ended, such as stickers, markers, and stamps, and let the child lead the pace over one or two sittings. Parents often expect only love and excitement here, so coach them beforehand to welcome whatever the child brings, including anger, and to avoid rushing past hard feelings toward reassurance.

fields.label: Draw or write one thing you like about having a new baby at home.
Draw or write one thing that feels hard or annoying about it.
Draw a time you felt left out or wanted more attention.
Draw or write one job a big sibling gets to do that a baby can't.
What is one thing you want your parent to know about how you feel?

title: New Parent Ask-for-Help Bingo
summary: A bingo game where new parents mark off small tasks they are willing to hand off to their support network.
goal: Use it to make delegating help feel playful instead of like admitting failure.
body_md: In a new-parent group, hand out bingo cards filled with squares like a meal drop-off, an hour of baby holding, a load of laundry, or a grocery run, and have each player mark a square once they name a specific person they could ask. Play a round where players share out loud what stopped them from asking before, since guilt, pride, and not wanting to seem like they can't cope come up often. Debrief by asking each player to pick one square to actually ask for before the group meets again.

fields.label: Which square was hardest for you to imagine asking for, and why?
Who is one person you could realistically ask this week?
What do you usually tell yourself when you consider asking for help?
What would you say to a friend who felt guilty asking for the same thing?
What is the one square you're committing to ask for before we meet again?

title: New Parent Identity Shift Worksheet
summary: A worksheet that helps a new parent name what has changed and what still feels like them since becoming a parent.
goal: Use it to normalize the identity change that often comes with early parenthood.
body_md: New parents often arrive describing a loss of self they can't quite name, caught between loving the baby and grieving parts of their old life, work identity, or body. Use this worksheet to make that shift explicit rather than something to feel guilty about, and normalize that identity change after birth can take a year or more to settle. Watch for clients who read any grief for their old life as evidence they are bad parents; the goal is naming the shift, not resolving it in one session.

fields.label: What is one part of your life before the baby that you miss?
What is one part of yourself that feels unfamiliar since becoming a parent?
What is one part of your old self that is still fully there?
What is something about this new version of you that you're starting to like?
What would you want to say to the person you were a year ago?

title: Bases of Self-Worth Pie Chart
summary: A CBT pie chart exercise mapping how much a client's sense of worth rests on each part of their life.
goal: Use it to show a client how narrowly their self-worth is resting on one or two areas.
body_md: Have the client list every area their self-worth currently rests on, such as work performance, appearance, being liked, or being a good parent, then draw a pie chart sizing each slice by how much weight it actually carries day to day. Most clients discover one or two oversized slices doing all the work, which explains why a single setback in that area can tank their mood. Follow up by sketching a second, more balanced pie together and naming small ways to grow the underused slices over time.

fields.label: List every area your sense of worth currently depends on.
Draw a pie chart sizing each area by how much it actually affects your mood.
Which slice is doing the most work, and what happens to you when it wobbles?
What is one underused area you'd like to grow?
What would a more balanced pie chart look like for you?

title: The Not Good Enough Story Defusion
summary: An ACT defusion exercise that helps a client notice and unhook from a familiar not-good-enough story.
goal: Use it to loosen the grip of a chronic self-judgment without arguing it true or false.
body_md: Have the client name their version of the story in a few words, then practice noticing it as a mental habit with a name rather than a fact, saying I'm having the not good enough story again instead of I am not good enough. Repeat it slowly, in a silly voice, or written on a card the client can hold up, so the words lose some of their pull. Some clients resist because the story feels true and dropping it feels like giving up standards; clarify that defusion changes their relationship to the thought, not whether it's accurate.

fields.label: In a few words, what is your version of the not-good-enough story?
When does this story tend to show up loudest?
What does the story usually make you do or avoid?
Say the story out loud starting with I'm having the thought that. How does that feel different?
If the story showed up but you didn't have to obey it, what would you do instead?

title: Non-Judgmental Self-Talk Practice
summary: A DBT mindfulness exercise that trains a client to describe themselves without judgment-laden labels.
goal: Use it to build the habit of a non-judgmental stance toward the client's own behavior and choices.
body_md: Ask the client to describe a recent moment they judged themselves harshly, first in their usual judgmental words, then again using only observable facts, stripping out words like stupid, lazy, or failure. This is harder than it sounds, since judgment often feels like the truth rather than an add-on, so model the rewrite together the first few times. Clients with a loud self-critic may resist, worried that dropping judgment means dropping standards or accountability; clarify that facts can still guide a change in behavior without the insult attached.

fields.label: Describe a moment you judged yourself harshly, in your usual words.
Now describe the same moment using only facts, no judgment words.
What judgment word did you catch yourself using most?
What would you say to a friend who described the same facts about themselves?
What is one non-judgmental phrase you could use next time this comes up?

title: How My Partner Sees Me Exercise
summary: A couples exercise where each partner writes down strengths they see in the other to counter one-sided self-criticism.
goal: Use it to give a client external evidence against their self-critical view, drawn from someone who knows them well.
body_md: Have each partner privately list strengths and qualities they admire in the other, then read the list aloud while the receiving partner simply listens without deflecting or arguing the points. Clients with low self-esteem often want to correct or minimize what they hear, so coach the receiving partner beforehand to practice just saying thank you. This works best paired with a brief talk about how one partner's self-esteem can quietly shape the relationship, so the listening partner understands why this exercise matters.

fields.label: List three strengths or qualities you admire in your partner.
Describe a specific moment your partner showed one of these strengths.
As the listener, what was hard about hearing this without arguing it?
What is one thing on this list that surprised you?
What is one strength you'd like your partner to remind you of on a hard day?

title: Pride Shield Building Craft
summary: A craft where a child builds and decorates a paper shield with things they're proud of about themselves.
goal: Use it to give a child a concrete, visible reminder of their own strengths.
body_md: The child cuts and decorates a shield shape, dividing it into sections for things like something I'm good at, something kind I did, and something I tried even though it was hard. Parents help by adding an observation of their own in one section, since children with low self-esteem often can't generate examples alone and need a prompt from someone who knows them. Send the shield home to hang somewhere visible, and coach the parent to reference it in passing rather than turning it into a lecture.

fields.label: Draw or write one thing you're good at.
Draw or write one kind thing you did for someone.
Draw or write one hard thing you tried, even if it didn't go perfectly.
Ask your grown-up to write one thing they're proud of you for.
Where will you hang your shield so you can see it?

title: Small Talk Roulette
summary: A group game where players spin for a small-talk prompt and practice starting a brief conversation.
goal: Use it to give clients low-stakes reps at initiating conversation before trying it outside session.
body_md: Players take turns spinning or drawing a prompt card, like asking about a weekend or commenting on the weather, then practice delivering it to a partner for thirty seconds before switching. Keep the first round low-pressure by letting players pass once, since the fear of freezing up is often the biggest barrier, not the content of what to say. In the debrief, ask what physical sensations came up and how the actual conversation compared to what they predicted beforehand, since predictions in social anxiety usually run far worse than reality.

fields.label: Which prompt felt easiest to deliver, and which felt hardest?
What did you predict would happen before you spoke?
What actually happened when you spoke?
What physical sensations came up while you waited your turn?
What is one small-talk opener you'd be willing to try outside this room?

title: Spotlight Effect Reality Check
summary: A worksheet that compares how closely a client thinks others noticed a mistake with how much they likely actually did.
goal: Use it to loosen the belief that others are watching and judging as closely as it feels.
body_md: Walk the client through a recent moment they felt embarrassed in public, having them rate how much they believe others noticed and remembered it, then compare that to how much they themselves remember about other people's small stumbles from the same week. Most clients draw a blank trying to recall others' minor mishaps, which makes the point better than explaining it would. Some clients argue their situation was different or worse; stay curious rather than debating, and let the exercise do the work over a few repetitions.

fields.label: Describe a recent moment you felt embarrassed in front of others.
On a scale of 0 to 100, how much do you think others noticed and remembered it?
Now think of someone else's small stumble this week. How much do you remember about it?
What does that gap suggest about how closely people are actually watching you?
What would you tell a friend who was sure everyone noticed their mistake?

title: Social Risk-Taking Experiment Log
summary: A CBT log for testing a specific social prediction against what actually happens when a client takes the risk.
goal: Use it to replace avoidance with small, testable social risks and real feedback.
body_md: Have the client pick one small social risk to try this week, like asking a question in a meeting or texting a friend first, and write down their prediction before doing it, including how bad they expect it to feel and for how long. After the attempt, they log what actually happened and how long any discomfort lasted, which is usually far shorter than predicted. Review the gap together in session rather than letting the client dismiss a good outcome as luck; the pattern across several logs is what shifts the belief, not any single entry.

fields.label: What is the small social risk you're going to try this week?
What do you predict will happen, and how bad do you expect it to feel?
How long do you predict the discomfort will last?
What actually happened when you tried it?
How long did the discomfort actually last, compared to your prediction?

title: They're All Judging Me Defusion Drill
summary: An ACT defusion drill for the automatic thought that everyone in a room is judging the client.
goal: Use it to help a client notice the judging thought as a mental habit rather than a fact about the room.
body_md: Have the client bring to mind a room where the everyone's judging me thought shows up loudest, then repeat the thought slowly out loud several times until the words start to lose their usual pull, a classic defusion technique. Follow it by having the client name the thought as a visitor, saying there's the judging thought again rather than treating it as news about the room. Some clients push back that the thought protects them from getting hurt; validate the function without agreeing the thought is accurate, and steer back toward what they'd do if the thought were just background noise.

fields.label: What room or situation does the everyone's judging me thought hit hardest in?
Say the thought out loud slowly, several times. What happens to it?
What does this thought usually get you to do or avoid?
If this thought showed up but you didn't have to listen to it, what would you do?
What is one value you'd be moving toward if you let the thought just pass through?

title: Participate Skill for Mingling
summary: A DBT mindfulness exercise using the participate skill to help a client engage in a social setting without over-planning.
goal: Use it to shift a client out of scripting every word in advance and into the moment instead.
body_md: Before a planned social event, have the client practice the participate skill by picking one low-stakes activity, like a short walk-and-talk with a friend, and entering it without a script, letting themselves act without extensive pre-planning. Debrief afterward on what came up when they weren't rehearsing lines in their head, since clients with social anxiety often over-plan as a safety behavior that keeps them half out of the conversation. Note where the urge to script returned strongest, since that's usually the spot worth practicing again.

fields.label: What social moment are you going to practice entering without a script?
What did you notice when you weren't rehearsing what to say?
Where did the urge to plan ahead come back strongest?
What happened in the conversation that you couldn't have scripted anyway?
What would it look like to participate this way again next week?

title: Grief Pace Mismatch Map
summary: Compares how each partner grieves and paces so neither reads the other's quiet as indifference.
goal: Turn a mismatch in grieving styles into a shared plan instead of a silent wedge between partners.
body_md: One partner may cry and talk, the other go quiet and stay busy; each can read the other's style as not caring. Have each partner describe their own pattern first, then guess the other's before checking it against what their partner actually wrote. Focus on what each one needs from the other during a hard stretch, not on making the styles match.

fields.label: How I grieve, in my own words
How I think my partner grieves
What I've assumed about my partner's quiet stretches
What I actually need from my partner when I'm grieving hard
What my partner actually needs from me when they're grieving hard
One thing we'll do differently around a hard date

title: Memory Quilt Square Craft
summary: A child decorates a paper square about the person who died, later joined with squares from the rest of the family.
goal: Give a grieving child something to make and a way into the family's shared mourning, not just their own.
body_md: Give the child paper, fabric scraps, markers and glue, and let them choose colors, words or small objects that remind them of the person; there is no wrong square. Coach the parent or caregiver to make their own square alongside the child rather than direct the child's. Join the finished squares into one quilt or poster the family can see, and bring it out again on birthdays or the anniversary.

fields.label: What's on my square, and why I picked it
A color I used and what it means to me
A memory that goes with my square
What I noticed on someone else's square
Where I want our quilt to hang

title: Guess Who Remembers Game
summary: Family members write memories of the person who died anonymously, then the group guesses who wrote each one.
goal: Show a grieving family how differently each person loved and remembers the same person.
body_md: Each player writes two or three short memories on cards without a name, or dictates them to the clinician if too young to write; shuffle the cards and read them aloud one at a time while the group guesses the author. There are no wrong guesses and no scorekeeping. Debrief on which memory surprised the group and what it showed about the person that no single member knew alone.

fields.label: The memories I wrote
A memory I guessed correctly
A memory that surprised me
My favorite memory someone else shared
Something I learned about the person I didn't know before

title: Secondary Losses Inventory
summary: Lists the roles, routines and plans that changed under the main loss, which grief work often skips past.
goal: Name the layered losses under the death itself so the work doesn't stall on the obvious loss alone.
body_md: Clients usually name only the death itself; ask directly what else changed under it: a role (spouse, caregiver, only child), a routine, an income, a plan for the future, a sense of identity. Each secondary loss can be grieved on its own terms and often explains a reaction that seems disproportionate to the main loss. Revisit the list as new secondary losses surface over the following months.

fields.label: The main loss
A role of mine that changed because of it
A routine or plan that no longer applies
A part of how I see myself that shifted
Which of these hits hardest right now
One person who can help with one item on this list

title: If-Only Thoughts Log
summary: Catches the if-only and should-have thoughts that follow a loss and tests them against what was knowable then.
goal: Loosen guilt attached to a choice the client could not have made differently with what they knew then.
body_md: Grief often comes with a running list of things the client believes they should have said, noticed or done differently. For each one, log the thought, then separate what the client actually knew at that moment from what only became clear in hindsight. Rate belief in the thought before and after; expect it to drop slowly rather than all at once, and repeat with new if-only thoughts as they surface.

fields.label: The if-only or should-have thought
How much I believe it right now (0-100%)
What I actually knew at that moment
What I only learned afterward, with hindsight
A fairer statement about that moment
How much I believe the fairer statement now (0-100%)

title: Partner Story Defusion Drill
summary: Separates what a partner actually did from the story the mind adds about what it means.
goal: Help the client respond to a partner's actual behavior instead of the mind's interpretation of it.
body_md: Pick a recent moment that stung. Have the client write the bare facts first, only what a camera would have recorded, then write the story the mind built on top: what it means about the partner, the relationship, or them. Say the story aloud with a defusion frame like 'I'm having the thought that' and notice it loosen. The facts rarely need as strong a reaction as the story does.

fields.label: The moment (bare facts only, like a camera would see it)
The story my mind added about what it means
Saying it as 'I'm having the thought that...' plus the story
What changes about the moment once I say it that way
How I want to respond to the facts alone

title: Ask Priorities Check for Partners
summary: Weighs getting the outcome, keeping the relationship and keeping self-respect before a hard ask of a partner.
goal: Help the client choose how hard to push a request based on what matters most to them this time.
body_md: Before scripting the ask itself, have the client rank three priorities for this particular request: getting the outcome, protecting the relationship, and keeping their own self-respect. A request about splitting chores might weigh differently than one about a boundary that was crossed. The ranking changes how firm, how soft, and how much the client is willing to give up to get it, and prevents an ask that wins the point but costs the relationship.

fields.label: What I want to ask my partner for
How much getting this outcome matters (1-10)
How much protecting the relationship matters here (1-10)
How much my own self-respect matters here (1-10)
Which priority wins if I have to choose
How that changes what I'll say

title: Negative Sentiment Check for Partners
summary: Tests whether a partner is reading neutral or kind moves as negative because goodwill has worn thin.
goal: Catch a flipped lens before it colors every interaction, so repair can start there and not just on the fights.
body_md: List several genuinely neutral or mildly positive things the partner did this week: texted a reminder, loaded the dishwasher a certain way, came home a few minutes late. Have each partner rate how they read it in the moment: neutral, kind, or as a dig. A pattern of reading neutral acts as hostile signals negative sentiment override, and the couple needs to rebuild goodwill before content-level fixes like scripts or chore charts will hold.

fields.label: Something neutral or kind my partner did this week
How I read it in the moment
How I'd read the same thing on a good week
What tells me goodwill is running low right now
One thing we'll do this week to rebuild it

title: Friendship Repair Recipe Card
summary: A child builds a step-by-step recipe card for repairing a fight with a friend.
goal: Give a child a concrete order of steps to follow after a friendship fight instead of freezing or avoiding.
body_md: Have the child decorate an index card with numbered steps in their own words and pictures, such as calm down first, say what happened, say sorry for their part, ask what the friend needs, and plan something fun together. Keep the parent's role to rehearsing the card with the child at home before it's needed and prompting 'what's step one?' in the moment rather than solving the fight for them.

fields.label: Step 1 on my card
Step 2 on my card
Step 3 on my card
A fight I could use my card for
Who can practice this with me at home

title: Repair Attempt Roleplay Round
summary: Partners rehearse mid-argument repair phrases on low-stakes scripted scenarios before they need them live.
goal: Make repair attempts automatic under mild stress instead of something a partner has to invent mid-fight.
body_md: Write several mild, scripted disagreement scenarios on cards beforehand. One partner draws a card and plays a lightly escalating role while the other practices deploying a repair attempt from an agreed list: a raised hand, a code word, a moment of humor. Swap roles each round. Keep the scenarios genuinely low-stakes; the goal is rehearsal, not reopening a real fight. Debrief on which repair attempts felt natural and which felt forced.

fields.label: The scenario I drew
The repair attempt I tried
How my partner responded to it
A repair attempt that felt natural to me
A repair attempt that felt forced
The one I want to use for real this week

title: Session Pacing Agreement
summary: Agreed signals a client can use in session to slow down, pause or stop without having to explain why.
goal: Give a survivor real control over pace before deeper work begins, not just control in principle.
body_md: Complete this together in session, not as homework. Agree on a pause word or hand signal, what the clinician will do when it's used, and how often to check in during harder stretches of work. Ask what it looks like when the client freezes or goes quiet rather than using the signal, since that is common, and agree on what the clinician should do then. This sheet does not ask for any detail about what happened.

fields.label: My pause word or signal
What I want you to do when I use it
What it looks like when I freeze instead of signaling
What I want you to do if that happens
How often I want you to check in during harder work
What I want to decide is always my choice

title: Safety Judgment Continuum
summary: Rates how safe specific present-day people and situations actually are against a blanket no-one-is-safe alarm.
goal: Loosen an all-or-nothing danger belief without asking the client to revisit what happened.
body_md: Stay entirely in the present for this one. List specific people or situations from the client's current life and have them rate each one's danger from 0 to 100, then note what evidence supports and challenges that rating. Survivors often carry an all-or-nothing alarm that reads everyone as equally unsafe; the continuum makes the real differences visible. Do not ask for any account of the past event itself.

fields.label: A person or situation from my life right now
My danger rating for it (0-100)
Evidence that supports this rating
Evidence that challenges this rating
A more accurate rating
What's actually different about the people I rate as safer

title: Then Versus Now Anchoring Practice
summary: Uses present-moment senses to mark the difference between the danger that happened then and the safety here now.
goal: Build a fast, rehearsed way back to the present when a reminder pulls the client into the past.
body_md: Practice this while calm, well before it's needed live, and never as a way to draw out the narrative; the point is contrast, not content. Have the client name, in general terms only, one thing true of 'then' and pair it with something only true of 'now': this room, this year, this choice, this body at an age it wasn't then. Anchor the 'now' side to a physical action like planting both feet, and rehearse the pairing until it's quick.

fields.label: One thing true of 'then,' in general terms only
One thing only true of 'now'
My physical anchor for 'now' (feet, hands, breath)
A word or phrase that means 'now' to me
When I'll practice this on purpose this week

title: Body Alarm Radical Acceptance Practice
summary: Applies radical acceptance to the body's leftover alarm reactions so the client stops fighting a response it can't outthink.
goal: Reduce the added suffering of judging a startle or freeze reaction as wrong or broken.
body_md: A startle, a freeze, a flinch at an ordinary touch: these are the body's alarm system doing its job late, not a sign anything is currently wrong with the client. Log the reaction, then the judgment the mind adds about it, then a radical acceptance statement that names the reaction as understandable given the body's history without agreeing it means danger now. Pair with one self-soothe step. Fighting the reaction tends to prolong it; naming it tends to let it pass.

fields.label: The reaction (startle, freeze, flinch...)
What my mind says about having this reaction
A radical acceptance statement about it
One self-soothe step I used afterward
How long the reaction lasted this time

title: Partner Support and Pace Agreement
summary: Agreed roles for a partner supporting a survivor: what helps, what to avoid, and who sets the pace for touch.
goal: Turn a partner's wish to help into welcomed, concrete actions instead of guesses that can retraumatize.
body_md: Complete this together in session, and keep it about present-day needs, not the history of what happened. Cover touch and how the survivor wants to signal not now, how the partner should check in without hovering, what to do if the survivor freezes or goes somewhere else in their mind, and how the partner manages their own hurt or frustration without asking the survivor to reassure them. Review it again after it's been tried.

fields.label: Touch or closeness that feels okay right now
How I'll signal 'not now' to my partner
How I want my partner to check in without hovering
What my partner should do if I freeze or go quiet
Where I'll take my own hard feelings instead of to you
When we'll revisit this agreement

title: Coping Toolbox Craft
summary: A shoebox a child paints and fills with drawn or written reminders of their go-to coping skills.
goal: Give a child a hands-on reminder of the coping skills they can reach for when big feelings hit.
body_md: Bring a small box, paper, markers, and glue to session. The child decorates the outside as their own toolbox, then fills it with slips naming or drawing skills that help them calm down, like squeezing a stress ball or taking slow breaths. Some children want to fill it with small toys instead of paper; let them, and write the skill on a tag tied to each item. Send the box home and ask the parent to keep it somewhere the child can reach it alone.

fields.label: Draw or write one thing that helps you calm your body.
Draw or write one thing that helps you calm your mind.
Who is someone you can go to when you need help calming down?
Where will you keep your toolbox so you can find it fast?

title: Coping Skill Swap
summary: A trading-card game where players swap coping skills that fit different feelings and situations.
goal: Build a wider coping repertoire by having players teach each other what actually works for them.
body_md: Each player writes three coping skills they already use on index cards, one per card, then the group mixes all the cards into a shared deck. Players take turns drawing a card and describing a moment when that skill would help, then decide whether to keep it or trade it back in. Round out the game with a debrief on which traded skills people plan to actually try, and which ones only sound good on paper. Works well in a group session or with a family stuck using the same one or two skills.

fields.label: Which three coping skills did you bring to the deck?
Which skill did you trade for, and why did it catch your attention?
What situation would you try a new skill in this week?
Which skill sounds good but you're not sure you'd actually use?

title: Coping Skill Effectiveness Tracker
summary: A log where a client rates how well each coping skill actually worked in the moment.
goal: Help a client tell which coping skills earn a place in their routine and which ones fall flat.
body_md: After each stressful moment this week, the client jots the situation, the skill they tried, and a quick rating of how much it helped. Bring the sheet back to session and sort the skills into a short list worth repeating and a longer list to retire or adapt. Watch for clients who rate everything as unhelpful because they tried the skill mid-crisis instead of practicing it beforehand; that pattern is worth naming out loud rather than written off as a failed skill.

fields.label: What was the situation?
Which coping skill did you try?
How much did it help, from not at all to a lot?
What would you do differently next time?

title: Problem vs Emotion-Focused Coping Sort
summary: A sorting exercise that separates a client's coping list into problem-focused and emotion-focused strategies.
goal: Show a client when to fix the situation directly and when to focus on managing the feeling instead.
body_md: The client lists recent stressors, then sorts their usual responses into two columns: strategies that change the situation and strategies that change how they feel about it. Many clients lean heavily on one column, using problem-solving on things they cannot control or trying to feel calmer about something they could actually change. Use the sheet to match the strategy to what the stressor allows, and to notice stressors that call for both columns at once.

fields.label: List a stressor from the past week.
What could you do to change or fix this situation directly?
What could help you feel calmer about it, even if it can't be fixed?
Which column does this stressor mostly call for?

title: Coping Strategy Workability Check
summary: A check-in that asks whether a coping strategy moves a client toward their values or just away from pain.
goal: Help a client judge coping strategies by workability instead of by whether they simply feel better.
body_md: For each coping strategy the client names, walk through three questions: does it help in the moment, does it still help the next day, and does it move them toward the life they want or away from it. A strategy can pass the first question and fail the other two, and that gap is the useful part of the conversation. Use it with clients who already have a long coping list but keep reaching for the same short-term fix under pressure.

fields.label: Name a coping strategy you use often.
Does it help in the moment? How?
How does it feel the next day, or a week later?
Does it move you toward or away from what matters to you?

title: Opposite Action for Phobias Card
summary: A pocket card that walks a client through opposite action when fear urges them to avoid a specific trigger.
goal: Give a client a quick script for approaching a feared object or situation instead of automatically avoiding it.
body_md: Fill the card out together for one specific feared trigger, naming the avoidance urge and a small, all-the-way opposite action the client can actually do. The client carries the card and reads it before or during a planned approach, checking that the action is done fully rather than half-heartedly, since a hesitant approach tends to reinforce the fear instead of easing it. This pairs well with a graded plan rather than the client's single scariest step first.

fields.label: What is the specific thing you're afraid of?
What does the fear urge you to do (avoid, leave, check)?
What is the all-the-way opposite action you'll practice?
How will you know you did the full action, not a partial one?

title: Fear Support Script for Partners
summary: A worksheet where each partner writes what actually helps and what backfires when fear takes over.
goal: Turn a well-meaning partner's guesswork into a script both people agree on before the next scared moment.
body_md: Partner A describes their fear trigger and what support looks like when it hits, from words to say to whether they want to be touched or given space. Partner B writes what they currently do, and the two compare notes, since partners often default to reassurance, distraction, or pushing to approach faster, and any of those can help one person and frustrate another. Agree on a short script for Partner B to use next time and a signal Partner A can give for what they need in that moment.

fields.label: Partner A: what does your fear look like from the outside?
Partner A: what helps you most in that moment?
Partner B: what do you usually do when this happens?
Together: write the script Partner B will try next time.

title: Fear Monster Shrinking Craft
summary: A child draws their fear as a monster, then shrinks a new version of it after each brave step.
goal: Give a child a visual way to see a specific fear get smaller as they practice approaching it.
body_md: The child draws their feared thing as a big, detailed monster on a large sheet, naming what makes it scary. After each practiced brave step toward the real trigger, the child draws a smaller version of the monster on a fresh sheet, and the set is taped up in size order. Some children want to give the monster a silly name or voice, which is fine and often loosens the fear's grip. Ask the parent to keep the drawings visible at home and to point to the row whenever the child manages a new step.

fields.label: Draw your scary thing as a monster. What makes it feel big?
What is one small step you could try toward it?
Draw the monster again after your step. Is it smaller?
What would help the monster get even smaller next time?

title: Courage Ladder Dice Game
summary: A dice game where each roll sends a player up or down a printed ladder of approach steps toward a feared trigger.
goal: Turn a graded approach plan into a low-pressure game that keeps a client moving toward their trigger.
body_md: Before play, the client and clinician list five to eight approach steps toward one feared trigger, from easiest to hardest, and number them as rungs on a paper ladder. On their turn, a player rolls a die and moves that many rungs up, describing out loud how it would feel to do that step, and an optional rule sends a nervous player back one rung to retry an easier description. End with a debrief on which rungs felt easiest to talk through and which ones need more practice before they're attempted for real.

fields.label: List your steps from easiest to hardest, one per rung.
Which rung was easiest to talk through today?
Which rung made your body react the most?
What would help you feel ready to try that rung for real?

title: Phobia Trigger and Avoidance Map
summary: A map of one specific fear, the situations it touches, and every workaround a client uses to dodge it.
goal: Show a client how far a single fear has spread into their routines through avoidance and workarounds.
body_md: In the center, the client names the specific feared thing, then draws spokes out to every situation it touches, from the obvious to the roundabout, like driving an extra ten minutes to skip a bridge. Next to each spoke, they note the workaround they use to avoid it. The map usually turns out bigger than clients expect, and that surprise is useful groundwork for building an approach plan, since it shows how much room avoidance has been given rather than kept small.

fields.label: Name the specific thing you're afraid of.
List a situation this fear touches.
What do you do to avoid or work around it?
How much extra time or effort does that workaround cost you?

title: Appearance Thought Record
summary: A thought record that captures the automatic thought, feeling, and behavior right after a hard appearance moment.
goal: Help a client catch and question the automatic thoughts that fire in a hard appearance moment.
body_md: Right after a moment the client notices judging their appearance, they log the situation, the automatic thought, the feeling it brought, and what they did next, like changing clothes again or canceling plans. In session, work through the thought the way any automatic thought gets questioned: what's the evidence, what would they tell a friend thinking this, and what's a more balanced version. Watch for clients who use the record to keep dwelling on their appearance; the point is to catch the thought, not to keep looking.

fields.label: What was the situation?
What thought went through your mind about your appearance?
What did you feel, and how strong was it?
What did you do next?
What's a more balanced way to think about that moment?

title: Values Beyond Appearance Sort
summary: A card sort that separates a client's real values from the appearance rules they've mistaken for values.
goal: Help a client notice how much of their day serves appearance rules rather than what actually matters to them.
body_md: The client sorts a mixed set of value cards and appearance-rule cards, like looking a certain way or collecting compliments, into what genuinely matters to them versus what they've absorbed as a rule to follow. Many clients place appearance rules in the values pile at first, and that mix-up is the useful part of the conversation. Move into a short discussion of what time and energy would look like if the appearance rules loosened their grip and the sorted values led instead.

fields.label: Sort each card: is this a value or a rule you've picked up?
Which appearance rule takes up the most of your time or energy?
Which value would you like to give more room to?
What's one small action this week that serves that value?

title: Radical Acceptance Body Practice
summary: A guided practice that walks a client through radically accepting their body as it is right now.
goal: Help a client stop the exhausting fight against how their body looks and move toward acceptance instead.
body_md: Lead the client through the usual radical acceptance steps, but anchored to a specific appearance thought they keep fighting, noticing where the fight shows up in their body and breath. Acceptance here means dropping the internal argument, not approval or giving up on caring for themselves, and that distinction is worth naming clearly since clients often hear acceptance as surrender. Some clients need to practice this daily for weeks before the fight quiets even briefly, so frame one session as a start, not a finish.

fields.label: What appearance thought do you keep fighting?
Where do you feel that fight in your body?
What would it mean to stop fighting it, just for now?
What's one thing acceptance does NOT mean for you here?

title: Body Image Support Script for Partners
summary: A worksheet where partners agree on what to say, and what to avoid saying, about appearance.
goal: Replace guesswork with an agreed script so a partner's comments help instead of landing wrong.
body_md: Partner A names the comments about appearance that help, from a simple compliment to no comment at all, and the ones that sting even when well-intended, like reassurance that turns into a comparison. Partner B shares comments they've been unsure about offering and why. Together, the couple writes a short list of go-to phrases Partner B can use and a signal Partner A can give when a conversation about appearance needs to stop. Revisit the list after a few weeks, since what helps often shifts.

fields.label: Partner A: what comments about your appearance actually help?
Partner A: what comments land wrong, even when well-meant?
Partner B: what have you been unsure about saying?
Together: write two phrases Partner B can use going forward.

title: My Body Can Do Poster
summary: A poster where a child draws all the things their body lets them do, not how it looks.
goal: Help a child build a sense of their body as something that does things for them, not something to judge.
body_md: Give the child a large sheet and markers, and ask them to draw themselves doing things their body lets them do, like climbing, hugging, dancing, or running fast, one picture per section of the poster. Steer away from any drawing about how the body looks and toward what it does; if a child brings up comments they've heard about their appearance, gently note it and keep the poster focused on ability and action. Send the poster home and ask the parent to add a new drawing together each week.

fields.label: Draw something fun your body lets you do.
Draw something your body helped you do for someone else.
What is something new you'd like your body to help you try?
Who could you ask to try it with you?
